entry.title: How to Consume SAP Datasphere Analytical Models to SAP Fiori Using OData Services
entry.content:
Blog Co-Author by: Vinh Phat Tu

One of the common requirements in SAP Datasphere projects is exposing analytical models so they can be consumed by SAP Fiori applications or SAP CAP applications through OData services.

Although SAP Datasphere provides native capabilities to generate OData services for Analytical Models, the complete configuration requires several components working together:

  • SAP Datasphere
  • SAP BTP Destination Service
  • OAuth configuration
  • Trust between Datasphere and BTP
  • SAP CAP (optional)

In this blog, we will walk through the complete end-to-end configuration. By the end of this guide, you'll be able to expose your SAP Datasphere Analytical Model securely for SAP Fiori or any OData consumer.

 

Solution Architecture

The overall authentication flow is shown below:

SAP Datasphere
│
│ Generate OData Service
│
▼
OAuth Client (SAML Bearer)
│
▼
SAP BTP Destination
│
▼
SAP Fiori / SAP CAP Application

The authentication relies on:

  • OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion
  • Trusted Identity Provider
  • SAP BTP Destination Service


Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure you have:

  • SAP Datasphere Administrator access
  • SAP BTP Subaccount Administrator access
  • Destination Administration permissions
  • Analytical Model already deployed
  • Authorization to create OAuth Clients

Part 1: Configure SAP Datasphere

Step 1: Expose the Analytical Model for Consumption

In Data-Builder --> Select the Fact view of the Analytical model --> Enable Expose for Consumption

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 
 

Note: The Fact View (which is your final view for the analytical model) must be exposed — not just the Analytical Model itself. This makes the view available via OData.

 

Step 2: Establish Trust Between Datasphere and BTP

To enable secure token exchange between BTP and Datasphere, you need to establish a trust relationship.

1. In your BTP Subaccount (where the destination will be created), navigate to Security > Trust Configuration > Destination Trust.

2. In the Trust section, click Export to download the XML metadata file.

 

3. Open the XML file and note the Provider Name and Signing Certificate.

 

4. In SAP Datasphere, navigate to System > Administration > App Integration

  • Under Trusted Identity Providers, click Add a Trusted Identity Provider.
  • Enter the Provider Name and Signing Certificate from the exported XML file.

 

Step 3: Configure OAuth in SAP Datasphere

There are two approaches for setting up the OAuth connection: 
ApproachAuthentication TypeUse Case
API Access (Recommended)SAML 2.0 BearerSupports user propagation and delegated access
Technical UserClient CredentialsService-to-service without user context

To configure API Access (recommended):

  1. In Datasphere, go to System > Administration > App Integration.
  2. Click + Add an OAuth Client.

  1. Set the Purpose to API Access.
  2. Under Access, select:
    • Data Export Service (mandatory)
    • Catalog User API (optional)
    • Analytics Content Network Interaction (optional)
  3. Set the Authorization Type to SAML 2.0 Bearer.
  4. Save the configuration and note the Client ID and Client Secret.

 

Part 2: Create the BTP Destination

Navigate to your BTP Subaccount and go to Connectivity > Destinations > Create New Destination.
Configure the following properties:
PropertyValue
AuthenticationOAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion
Proxy TypeInternet
URLThe OData Service URL from your Analytical Model (see below)
Token Service URL

Found in Datasphere under System > Administration > OAuth2SAML Token URL

Important: Use the OAuth2SAML Token URL (not the standard OAuth Token URL) when using SAML 2.0 Bearer authentication.


Finding the OData Service URL:
  1. Open the Analytical Model you want to expose in Datasphere.
  2. Go to Tools > Generate OData Request.
  3. Copy the generated URL — this becomes the destination URL.

Note: Each Analytical Model requires its own BTP Destination, but you can reuse the same OAuth client across multiple destinations.

In BTP -> go to Subaccount -> Select 'Connectivity' -> Destinations -> Add New

Token Service Configuration

 
PropertyValue
Token Service URL TypeDedicated
Use Basic Credentials for Token ServiceEnabled
Token Service UserOAuth Client ID (from Datasphere)
Token Service PasswordOAuth Client Secret (from Datasphere)

 

SAML Properties

PropertyValue
AuthnContextClassRefurn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession
AudienceFound in Datasphere under App Integration (where OAuth was created)
Client KeyOAuth Client ID (Note: Client Key = Client ID, not the Secret)
SAML Assertion ProviderDestinationServiceGenerated
Name Id Formaturn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:emailAddress

 

Additional Properties

KeyValue
WebIDEEnabledTRUE
WebIDEUsageodata_gen
HTML5.DynamicDestinationTRUE
HTML5.SetXForwardedHeadersFALSE

 

 

Part 3: Consume the OData Service in an SAP CAP Application

Once the destination is configured and the Analytical Model is accessible via OData, you can consume it in an SAP CAP (Cloud Application Programming Model) application.
 
For a comprehensive deep dive, refer to the official CAPIRE documentation:

Consuming Services — SAP CAP Documentation

Prerequisites for CAP Integration

  • The $metadata file of the external OData service
  • A correctly configured BTP destination (completed in Part 2)

Step 1: Import the $metadata File into the CAP Project

The CAP framework needs to know the structure of the external OData service. Import the $metadata file using the CDS import command:

cds import <metadata_file> --as cds

This command performs the following:

  1. Creates an external folder inside the srv directory (or reuses it if it already exists)
  2. Copies the metadata file into the external folder
  3. Generates a .csn file based on the metadata (this defines the service structure for CDS)
  4. Adds an external service definition in package.json

 

 

Step 2: Review the External Service Definition in package.json

The CDS framework automatically adds an entry in package.json that points to the .csn file and specifies how to connect to the external OData service. For production, the connection uses the BTP destination. For local development, you can define a separate profile with a specific URL and credentials.

Step 3: Expose Entities from the External OData Service

To expose entities from the external service in your CAP application, add an import statement referencing the external .csn file using a relative path. Once imported, the external entities can be referenced like any regular CDS entity.

using { ExternalService } from './external/AnalyticalModel';

service MyService {

    entity AnalyticsData as projection on ExternalService.DataEntity;

}

 

Step 4: Add Custom Logic to Call the External OData Service

In your custom handler, use cds.connect.to to establish a connection to the external service. The parameter must match the service reference defined in package.json.

const cds = require('@sap/cds');

module.exports = cds.service.impl(async function () {

    const externalService = await cds.connect.to('ExternalServiceName');

    this.on('READ', 'AnalyticsData', async (req) => {

        return externalService.run(req.query);

    });

});

To call the external OData service, custom logic needs to be added in the respective custom handler for the CAP service. First a life cycle handler for the “on” phase for the respective entity needs to be defined. Afterwards the cds.connect.to command needs to be used. It uses one parameter to generate the client for the connection. The parameter is a string value and it needs to match the reference from the package.json file.  The resulting object is then used to run the query of the current request. After the function call, the promise is returned to the enclosing function to respond to the HTTP request and return the requested information.

 

Summary

To recap the end-to-end flow:

  1. Datasphere — Expose the Fact View for consumption and configure an OAuth client with SAML 2.0 Bearer authorization.
  2. BTP — Establish trust between the subaccount and Datasphere, then create a destination using OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion.
  3. CAP Application — Import the $metadata file, configure the service binding in package.json, and implement custom handlers to query the external OData service.

entry.title: Unplanned Items in Service Confirmations: An API Guide
entry.content:
When a technician arrives on-site and encounters work that falls outside the original service order scope — a part that needs replacing, an unexpected repair, labor not originally scheduled — that work still needs to be documented and financially accounted for. Service confirmations capture this reality, and unplanned items are the mechanism for recording work that was not pre-scheduled. This post focuses on how to create and manage unplanned items in service confirmations programmatically via external APIs, covering OData V2, OData V4, and SOAP. For each API, I explain how your Financial (FIN) integration mode shapes the payload and the expected system behavior, and provide concrete payload examples. Note that as of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition release 2025, the OData V2 service is deprecated and OData V4 is the recommended path for new integrations.

What Is an Unplanned Item? A Business Perspective

A service confirmation records the actual work performed during a service visit. When that work was planned in advance, the confirmation item traces back to a corresponding item in the service order — this is a planned item. Work that was not foreseen in the original order — an additional material consumed, an unexpected service rendered, or labor beyond the original estimate — needs to be captured separately. How this is modeled depends on your FIN integration mode.

With item-based accounting, this is where the concept of an unplanned item applies specifically: a confirmation item for which no preceding service order item existed, and for which the system automatically creates a new "unplanned" service order item as predecessor during confirmation creation. The term "Unplanned Item" in SAP is therefore tied to item-based accounting — it does not simply mean "work that was not planned," but refers to this specific creation pattern with a system-generated predecessor.

With legacy FIN integration, there is no equivalent named concept. Additional work is recorded as a standalone confirmation item, without a predecessor service order item. The distinction is not just terminological — it has direct consequences for cost allocation, billing, and financial reporting, as the API examples that follow demonstrate.

Creating Unplanned Items in the UI

Before diving into the APIs: the application for service confirmations provides direct UI support for creating unplanned items — though what is available depends on your FIN integration mode.

With item-based accounting active, the item list in the service confirmation overview includes an "Add Unplanned Item" button. Selecting it adds a new item to the service confirmation and automatically creates a predecessor service order item in the background. This button reflects the concept of an unplanned item as it is specifically defined in item-based accounting: an item initiated from within the service confirmation for which an "unplanned" service order item is created as predecessor.

Without item-based accounting (legacy FIN), this button does not exist. You simply create new items in the service confirmation directly — no predecessor service order item is required. The rest of this post focuses on replicating both behaviors via external APIs.

Finance Integration Modes: Legacy vs. Item-Based Accounting

The behavior when creating a service confirmation item — planned, unplanned, or standalone — depends on which FIN integration mode your system uses. Understanding this is essential before constructing any API payload.

Item-based accounting

In item-based accounting, the account assignment object resides at the service order item level. As a result, every service confirmation item must have a predecessor service order item — standalone confirmation items are not supported.

When creating a confirmation item via API, the field ReferenceServiceOrderItem acts as a template: the system uses it to automatically create a new predecessor service order item during the confirmation item creation. To designate the new item as unplanned, set RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned to true. If you omit this field, the system creates a planned item using the referenced order item as its predecessor.

Legacy FIN integration

With legacy FIN integration, RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned is optional, and its presence changes the outcome:

  • Set to true: The system creates a standalone confirmation item with no predecessor. Any value in ReferenceServiceOrderItem is disregarded.
  • Not set: The system creates a confirmation item with the service order item specified in ReferenceServiceOrderItem as its predecessor.

The tables below summarize expected system behavior and the required field values for each scenario. Both apply identically across all three APIs covered in this post.

Behavior by scenario and FIN integration mode:

#ScenarioItem-Based AccountingLegacy FIN Integration 
1Unplanned itemUnplanned item created; a new service order item is generated automatically as predecessorStandalone confirmation item created
2Planned itemConfirmation item created with predecessor service order itemSame as item-based accounting
3Standalone confirmation itemNot acceptedStandalone confirmation item created

Field values required to trigger each scenario:

#ScenarioReferenceServiceOrderItem RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned 
1Unplanned itemFilledtrue
2Planned itemFilledfalse
3Standalone confirmation itemEmptyNot relevant

Note: Scenario 3 is only valid under legacy FIN integration. Under item-based accounting, a confirmation item without a ReferenceServiceOrderItem is not accepted.

Creating Unplanned Items via OData V2

The OData V2 service for service confirmations is API_SERVICE_CONFIRMATION_SRV. Full technical details are available on the SAP API Business Hub.

Note: This OData V2 service is deprecated as of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition release 2025. For new integrations on release 2025 and higher, use the OData V4 service described in the next section.

To create a service confirmation including an unplanned item, send a POST request to the A_ServiceConfirmation entity set:

POST /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SERVICE_CONFIRMATION_SRV/A_ServiceConfirmation

Prerequisite: a service order in status "Released" with at least one service item (item 10 in this example).

The example below creates a service confirmation with two items in a single request: a planned item referencing service order item 10, and an unplanned item also using item 10 as a template with RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned set to true. Note the following V2-specific field names:

  • Items are embedded via the to_Item navigation property
  • The product field is named Product
  • The quantity unit field is named QuantityUnit

Replace the service order ID and executing service employee ID in the payload with values from your system.

Payload:

{
  "ServiceConfirmationType": "SRVC",
  "ServiceConfirmationDescription": "unplanned item",
  "Language": "EN",
  "ReferenceServiceOrder": "8000063358",
  "to_Item": [
    {
      "ReferenceServiceOrder": "8000063358",
      "ReferenceServiceOrderItem": "10"
    },
    {
      "ReferenceServiceOrder": "8000063358",
      "ReferenceServiceOrderItem": "10",
      "RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned": true,
      "Product": "SRV_02",
      "Quantity": "1",
      "QuantityUnit": "EA",
      "ExecutingServiceEmployee": "9980000543"
    }
  ]
}

Result — Item-based accounting: A service confirmation is created with two items. Item 10 is a service item with service order item 10 as predecessor. Item 20 is an expense item, and a new unplanned service order item is automatically created in the service order as its predecessor.

Result — Legacy FIN integration: A service confirmation is created with two items. Item 10 is a service item with service order item 10 as predecessor. Item 20 is an expense item without a predecessor (standalone item).

Creating Unplanned Items via OData V4

The OData V4 service for service confirmations is api_serviceconfirmation (srvd_a2x), available from SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition release 2025. Full technical details are available on the SAP API Business Hub. To create a service confirmation including an unplanned item, send a POST request to the ServiceConfirmation entity set:

POST /sap/opu/odata4/sap/api_serviceconfirmation/srvd_a2x/sap/serviceconfirmation/0001/ServiceConfirmation

Prerequisite: a service order in status "Released" with at least one service item (item 10 in this example).

The example below covers the same logical scenario as the V2 example above. Note the structural differences from V2 worth calling out in your integration:

  • Items are embedded via _ServiceConfirmationItem (not to_Item)
  • The product field is named OriginallyRequestedProduct (not Product)
  • The quantity unit field is named SrvcConfItmQuantityUnitISOCode (not QuantityUnit)

Replace the service order ID, RespEmployeeBusinessPartnerId, and ServiceEmployee values in the payload with values from your system.

Payload:

{
  "ServiceConfirmationType": "SRVC",
  "ServiceConfirmationDescription": "unplanned item",
  "Language": "EN",
  "ReferenceServiceOrder": "8000076824",
  "RespEmployeeBusinessPartnerId": "9980000000",
  "ServiceEmployee": "9980000000",
  "_ServiceConfirmationItem": [
    {
      "ReferenceServiceOrder": "8000076824",
      "ReferenceServiceOrderItem": "10"
    },
    {
      "ReferenceServiceOrder": "8000076824",
      "ReferenceServiceOrderItem": "10",
      "RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned": true,
      "OriginallyRequestedProduct": "SRV_02",
      "Quantity": 2.000,
      "SrvcConfItmQuantityUnitISOCode": "EA"
    }
  ]
}

Result — Item-based accounting: A service confirmation is created with two items. Item 10 is a service item with service order item 10 as predecessor. Item 20 is an expense item, and a new unplanned service order item is automatically created in the service order as its predecessor.

Result — Legacy FIN integration: A service confirmation is created with two items. Item 10 is a service item with service order item 10 as predecessor. Item 20 is an expense item without a predecessor (standalone item).

Creating Unplanned Items via SOAP

The SOAP-based service confirmation API is ServiceConfirmationRequest. Full technical details, including the WSDL and message type documentation, are available on the SAP API Business Hub.

The API operates asynchronously: the calling system sends the request message without receiving an immediate response containing the created document data. Set the fields as described in the FIN integration section above. In the SOAP message, RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned uses the string values true and false.

Two scenarios are shown below.

Unplanned Item / Standalone Item

Prerequisite: a service order in status "Released" with at least one service item (item 10 in this example).

Replace the service order ID in the payload with a value from your system.

<ServiceConfirmation actionCode="01">
    <ServiceConfirmationType>SRVC</ServiceConfirmationType>
    <ServiceConfirmationDescription languageCode="EN">Some description</ServiceConfirmationDescription>
    <ExternalDocLastChangeDateTime>2020-05-05T12:10:00.1234567Z</ExternalDocLastChangeDateTime>
    <ReferenceServiceOrder>8000025501</ReferenceServiceOrder>
    <Item actionCode="01">
        <Material>SRV_01</Material>
        <Quantity unitCode="hur">2</Quantity>
        <ServiceDuration unitCode="hur">0.4</ServiceDuration>
        <ReferenceServiceOrderItem>10</ReferenceServiceOrderItem>
        <RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned>true</RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned>
    </Item>
</ServiceConfirmation>

Result — Item-based accounting: A service confirmation is created with one service item. A new unplanned service order item is automatically created in the service order as its predecessor.

Result — Legacy FIN integration: A service confirmation is created with one service item without a predecessor service order item (standalone item).

Planned Item

Prerequisite: a service order with at least service item 10 in status "Released".

Replace the service order ID in the payload with a value from your system.

<ServiceConfirmation actionCode="01">
    <ServiceConfirmationType>SRVC</ServiceConfirmationType>
    <ServiceConfirmationDescription languageCode="EN">Some description</ServiceConfirmationDescription>
    <ExternalDocLastChangeDateTime>2020-05-05T12:10:00.1234567Z</ExternalDocLastChangeDateTime>
    <ReferenceServiceOrder>8000025501</ReferenceServiceOrder>
    <Item actionCode="01">
        <Quantity unitCode="hur">2</Quantity>
        <ServiceDuration unitCode="hur">0.4</ServiceDuration>
        <ReferenceServiceOrderItem>10</ReferenceServiceOrderItem>
        <RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned>false</RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned>
    </Item>
</ServiceConfirmation>

Result — both FIN integration modes: A service confirmation is created with one item with service order item 10 as predecessor.

Key Takeaways and Next Steps

Unplanned items in service confirmations follow a clear set of rules — but those rules differ significantly between FIN integration modes. Item-based accounting enforces predecessor relationships throughout and does not permit standalone items. Legacy FIN is more permissive and supports standalone confirmation items. The fields ReferenceServiceOrderItem and RefSrvcOrdItemIsUnplanned are the two levers that control the outcome in both models, though their effect differs between modes.

All three APIs — OData V2, OData V4, and SOAP — support unplanned item creation with the same underlying field logic. Your API choice should be driven by your integration architecture and communication pattern, not by the unplanned item functionality itself. For systems on release 2025 and higher, OData V4 is the recommended path as the V2 service is deprecated.

Working through a specific integration scenario or running into unexpected behavior? Drop a comment below — I am happy to discuss.

Further Reading

  • Unplanned Item — SAP S/4HANA Documentation
  • Service Order: Unplanned Item in SAP S/4HANA Cloud — SAP Community Blog

entry.title: Managing Contract Attachments in SAP SRM Using OData Service
entry.content:
Introduction

 

 

While developing a Fiori application for SAP SRM Contract management, one of the requirements was to allow users to maintain contract attachments without opening SAP GUI.

The users wanted to perform the following operations directly from the application:

  • Upload a new attachment to an SRM Contract
  • Update the description of an existing attachment
  • Delete an existing attachment

The frontend application sends the uploaded file as a Base64 string, whereas the SAP SRM attachment framework expects the file content in binary format along with additional metadata such as GUID, MIME type, description, and visibility.

In this blog, I will explain how I implemented contract attachment management using a custom OData service and standard SAP SRM function modules.

Business Scenario

Consider a user working with an SRM Contract from a Fiori application.

The user uploads a new file, for example:

Contract_Amendment.pdf

The file is sent from the frontend as Base64 content.

The OData service receives this request, converts the file into the required format, prepares the attachment structure, updates the contract, validates the changes, and finally saves the attachment against the SRM Contract.

The same service is also used when the user wants to update an attachment description or remove an attachment.

Reading the Existing Document

Before making any changes, I first read the document along with its existing attachments.

CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PROCDOC_GETDETAIL_DIRECT'
  EXPORTING
    i_object_id   = lv_documentnumber
    i_object_type = gc_obj_bus2000113
    i_read_flags  = ls_read_flags
  IMPORTING
    e_header      = ls_header
    et_attach     = et_attach.

Here, BUS2000113 represents the SRM Contract object type.

Initially, I thought only the contract header information would be required. However, during testing, I realized that all attachment operations depend on the existing attachment collection.

The attachment table returned by this function is used as the base for:

  • Adding a new attachment
  • Updating an existing attachment description
  • Marking an attachment for deletion

Handling Multiple Operations with a Single Service

Instead of creating separate OData operations for upload, delete, and update, I used a single CREATE_ENTITY implementation.

The action received from the frontend determines which operation needs to be executed.

CASE ls_create-action.

  WHEN 'UPLOAD'.

  WHEN 'DELETE'.

  WHEN 'EDITDESC'.

ENDCASE.

This keeps both the frontend and backend simple. The frontend only calls one endpoint, and the backend decides which logic to execute.

Uploading the Attachment

When the file reaches the backend, it is still in Base64 format.

The first thing I do is convert it into an XSTRING.

DATA(lv_xstring_content) =
    cl_http_utility=>decode_x_base64(
        encoded = ls_create-filebase64 ).

The attachment framework cannot directly save Base64 data, so this conversion is mandatory.

Once the content is available, I generate a new GUID for the attachment.

CALL FUNCTION 'GUID_CREATE'

The GUID uniquely identifies the attachment inside the SRM document.

Why the MIME Type Is Important

One issue I encountered during testing was that some uploaded files were not recognized correctly when the MIME type was missing.

Instead of assigning a fixed value, I extract the file extension from the uploaded filename and determine the MIME type dynamically.

CALL FUNCTION 'SDOK_MIMETYPE_GET'

If no MIME type is returned, I assign application/pdf as a fallback.

This small check prevented several upload issues during testing.

Preparing the File for SRM

Although the file is now available as an XSTRING, the SRM attachment framework expects binary content.

For that reason, I convert it before appending it to the attachment table.

CALL FUNCTION 'SCMS_XSTRING_TO_BINARY'

After the conversion, I populate the remaining attachment fields and append the new attachment to the existing attachment collection.

At this point, nothing has been saved yet. The attachment is only prepared for the update process.

Updating or Deleting an Existing Attachment

For updating the description, I simply locate the attachment using its GUID and change the description field.

<fs_attach>-description = ls_create-description.

Deleting an attachment works a little differently.

Initially, I expected to remove the entry from the internal table. After checking how the SRM framework works, I found that SAP only expects the deletion indicator to be set.

<fs_attach>-del_ind = abap_true.

The framework removes the attachment automatically when the contract is saved.

Updating the Document

Once the attachment table reflects the required changes, I pass it to the contract update API.

CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PD_CTR_UPDATE'

This prepares the modified contract, but it does not immediately write anything to the database.

Before saving, I validate the contract.

CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PD_CTR_CHECK'

Only if no validation errors are returned do I proceed with the save.

CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PD_CTR_SAVE'.

COMMIT WORK AND WAIT.

This sequence ensures that attachment changes are saved only when the contract is in a consistent state.

The interesting part of this implementation was that the actual upload logic was only a small portion of the solution. Most of the work involved understanding how the SRM attachment framework expects attachment data to be prepared before it can be saved.

Using a single OData service for upload, delete, and description updates helped keep the implementation straightforward, while the standard SRM function modules handled the actual persistence and validation.

If you're implementing a similar requirement in SAP SRM, I hope this walkthrough gives you a good starting point.

entry.title: SAP OData Service Catalog Viewer
entry.content:
In one of the project discussions, we needed to figure out which APIs, or more specifically which OData services, were available in one of the SAP systems. While we can use transaction /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE to view and search for specific OData services, I wanted a simpler way to show the full service catalog in a web app. The app should display all available services and include a simple search field, along with filters for service type, release status, author, and whether it is an SAP service.

I created a very simple utility web app (used GHC to create it) that can help people within the organization browse the OData service catalog. First, users need to export the JSON payload from the query /sap/opu/odata/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE;v=2/ServiceCollection?$format=json and then upload it to this app https://chandrashekhar-mahajan.github.io/SAP-OData-Service-Catalog/

I intentionally kept it as a static-file app, since the goal is simply to understand which OData services are available and active in the SAP system. Try it and let me know your comments/feedback.

entry.title: Calling OData from SAP Screen Personas: Adding an EAN Field to an WM RF Screen in public cloud 2602
entry.content:
Introduction

Extending EWM RF screens is particularly challenging in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

The RF framework is standardised, and customers cannot freely enhance the RF flow or underlying Dynpro logic in the same way as in an private  system. Even a simple requirement such as displaying an additional product attribute could previously lead to a separate SAP BTP application or another side-by-side solution.

That may be justified when the additional information is part of the business logic. However, it can be excessive when the requirement is only to display an existing value to the warehouse operator.

When I first saw that GuiODataClient was available in SAP Screen Personas, I immediately thought that this could be a real game changer for classic applications in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Screen Personas scripting is based on JavaScript, so once an OData client is available, the range of possible lightweight UI extensions becomes significantly broader.

This approach allows us to:

  • keep the standard RF transaction;
  • avoid modifications to the RF application;
  • use a released SAP API;
  • display supplementary information without using it in the RF process logic.

At the same time, I found relatively few practical examples in the SAP documentation showing how to use this capability in a real business scenario. This article therefore focuses on one concrete EWM RF use case and shares the implementation pattern that worked for me. But of course could be applicable for wide range of cases.

The example below adds the main EAN/GTIN of the current product to an EWM RF receiving screen.

Scenario

The standard RF screen already contains the product number.

The requirement is to display the product’s main EAN in an additional read-only field.

The solution follows this flow:

 
Product number on the RF screen
        ↓
SAP Screen Personas script
        ↓
Released Product OData V4 API
        ↓
ProductStandardID
        ↓
Custom read-only EAN field
The EAN is used for information purposes only. It is not submitted back to the RF transaction and does not influence the RF process logic.

Prerequisites

The example assumes that:

  • SAP Screen Personas is available for the classic RF application;
  • session.createODataClient() is supported in the relevant SAP S/4HANA Cloud release;
  • the Product OData V4 service is active and accessible to the user;
  • the product master contains a value in ProductStandardID;
  • the user is authorised to read the product through the API.

The Product API service root used in this example is (could be checked on SAP API HUB

 
/sap/opu/odata4/sap/api_product/srvd_a2x/sap/product/0002/
Step 1: Add the custom EAN field

Open the RF screen in the SAP Screen Personas flavor editor and add:

  • a label, for example EAN;
  • a single-line text field for the value.

The generated Personas control ID in this example is:

 
wnd[0]/usr/txtPersonas_17851641694533

Configure the field as read-only, because the value is intended only for display.

The exact control ID will be different in another flavor or system. It can be identified using the Personas editor, object inspector, or script recorder.

My practical advice is not to expect every control ID to be documented or directly discoverable. Record a few interactions, compare the generated paths, and look for the program name, subscreen number, structure name, and field name inside the control ID. Once the pattern becomes clear, the rest is usually much easier.

Step 2: Create the Personas script

The script must:

  1. Confirm that it is currently running on the intended RF screen.
  2. Confirm that both the standard product field and the custom EAN field are available.
  3. Stop without an error on all other RF screens.
  4. Avoid an API request when the product field is empty.
  5. Read the current product from the RF screen.
  6. Call the released Product OData API.
  7. Read ProductStandardID.
  8. Write the result into the custom Personas field.
  9. Clear the field when the product or EAN is unavailable.

There is currently no clear, central reference that explains where to find the technical IDs of individual RF screen controls in SAP Screen Personas.

A practical way to identify them is to use the script recorder:

  1. Start recording a script.
  2. Click into fields, change values, press buttons, or navigate between RF steps.
  3. Review the generated script and compare which control IDs change.
  4. Use the structure of the IDs to identify the relevant program, subscreen, and field.

For example, the product field used in this scenario was identified as:

wnd[0]/usr/subX:/SCWM/SAPLRF_RECEIVING_HUS_PM:0401/txt/SCWM/S_RF_REHU_PROD-MATNR

This particular field was not exposed directly by the recorder in an obvious way. It was identified by combining the recorder output with general knowledge of the EWM RF framework and by comparing the structure with similar RF screens in on-premise systems.

A sample implementation is shown below.

const productFieldId =
    "wnd[0]/usr/subX:/SCWM/SAPLRF_RECEIVING_HUS_PM:0401/" +
    "txt/SCWM/S_RF_REHU_PROD-MATNR";

const eanFieldId =
    "wnd[0]/usr/txtPersonas_17851641694533";

let productField = null;let eanField = null;

/*
 * RF applications frequently reuse the same outer Dynpro
 * for several different logical RF screens.
 *
 * Therefore, first verify that the required controls exist.
 */
try {
    productField = session.findById(productFieldId);
    eanField = session.findById(eanFieldId);
} catch (controlError) {
    return;
}

/*
 * Depending on the runtime, findById may return undefined
 * instead of raising an exception.
 */
if (!productField || !eanField) {
    return;
}

/*
 * Read the product only after the controls have been verified.
 */
const product = String(productField.text || "").trim();

if (!product) {
    eanField.text = "";
    return;
}

try {
    const productClient = session.createODataClient(
        "/sap/opu/odata4/sap/api_product/" +
        "srvd_a2x/sap/product/0002/"    );

    const escapedProduct =
        product.replace(/'/g, "''");

    const requestUrl =
        "Product('" +
        escapedProduct +
        "')?$select=Product,ProductStandardID";

    const response = productClient.sendCustomRequest({
        url: requestUrl,
        method: "GET",
        headers: {
            "Accept": "application/json"        },
        body: ""    });

    const status = Number(response.status);

    if (status >= 200 && status < 300) {
        const productData = JSON.parse(
            response.responseText || "{}"        );

        const ean =
            productData.ProductStandardID || "";

        eanField.text = ean;
    } else {
        eanField.text = "";

        console.log(
            "EAN request failed:",
            response.status,
            response.responseText,
            response.error
        );
    }
} catch (requestError) {
    eanField.text = "";

    console.log(
        "Unexpected EAN lookup error:",
        requestError &&
        requestError.message
            ? requestError.message
            : String(requestError)
    );
}
Important implementation points

This example worked well for my scenario, but it should still be treated as a pattern rather than copied blindly. RF applications reuse screens and subscreens extensively, so the event behaviour, control IDs, API version, and empty-state handling should always be validated in the target system.

The most important part is the initial screen validation.

EWM RF transactions commonly use a shared outer screen, while the actual logical RF step is loaded into a subscreen. A script assigned to a refresh event may therefore run on multiple RF screens.

The script must not start by reading the product directly - If the field does not exist on the current RF step, this can result in an error such as: Сannot read properties of undefined

Instead, the controls must first be located and validated:

 

try {
    productField = session.findById(productFieldId);
    eanField = session.findById(eanFieldId);
} catch (error) {
    return;
}

if (!productField || !eanField) {
    return;
}

Only after that should the script read the product value and call the API.

The second important check is the empty product condition:

 
if (!product) {
    eanField.text = "";
    return;
}
This prevents unnecessary OData requests during intermediate screen refreshes where the RF screen is already displayed but the product has not yet been populated.

But please keep in mind that such screen change will affect on all warehouses.

Step 3: Assign the script to the screen event

The script should run automatically when the RF screen is populated.

For this scenario, assign the script to the appropriate screen lifecycle event in the flavor editor.

onAfterRefresh is often suitable for RF applications because the outer RF Dynpro may remain unchanged while the content of its subscreen is refreshed.

Typical configuration:

  1. Open the relevant flavor.
  2. Open the script event configuration.
  3. Select the EAN lookup script.
  4. Assign it to onAfterRefresh.
  5. Save and publish the flavor.

Depending on the RF flow and system behaviour, onLoad may also be sufficient. The correct event should be verified in the actual process.

The safety checks in the script are especially important when using onAfterRefresh, because the event may be triggered frequently and on RF steps where the product field does not exist.

 

Result

When the operator opens the relevant RF screen:

  1. The script checks that the expected product and EAN controls exist.
  2. It reads the product number from the standard RF field.
  3. It calls the released Product OData API.
  4. It retrieves ProductStandardID.
  5. It writes the value into the custom read-only EAN field.

On other RF screens, the required controls are not available, so the script exits without executing the OData request.

Why this approach fits the requirement

This solution is appropriate because the EAN is only displayed as supplementary information.

The custom field:

  • is not transferred back to the RF backend;
  • is not used to determine process steps;
  • does not change product master data;
  • does not replace RF validations;
  • does not influence posting or warehouse task creation.

The actual RF process remains standard.

If the additional value were required for process logic, validation, posting or navigation, a display-only Personas solution would not be sufficient. In that case, a released backend extension, custom application or other supported extensibility mechanism would still be required.

Security and performance considerations

Debugging

Personas scripts can be debugged conveniently in Google Chrome using the standard Developer Tools. The browser console is particularly useful for inspecting console.log() output, HTTP response statuses, OData response bodies, and JavaScript runtime errors.

Use released APIs

The solution uses a released OData API rather than direct table access, unreleased function modules or modifications to the RF backend.

Respect user authorisations

The OData request runs in the user’s session and is subject to the user’s authorisations.

Request only the required properties

The script requests only: ProductStandardID using: $select=Product,ProductStandardID

This keeps the response small and avoids retrieving unnecessary product master data.

Avoid unnecessary requests

The script exits before creating the OData client when:

  • the target RF controls are not present;
  • the product is empty.

Keep the added field read-only

The Personas field should only display the API result. It should not give the impression that editing it changes the product master or the RF document.

Conclusion

GuiODataClient creates a useful new extensibility option for classic applications in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.

For EWM RF scenarios, this is particularly valuable because standard RF flows offer limited customisation possibilities. Previously, even a small display requirement could lead to a separate SAP BTP application or another side-by-side extension.

In this example, the standard RF process remains unchanged. SAP Screen Personas reads the product from the existing screen, calls the released Product OData API and displays the EAN in a custom read-only field.

The approach is lightweight, based on released interfaces and suitable for supplementary information that is not part of the core RF process logic.

My main takeaway from this implementation is that the capability is more powerful than it may initially appear. SAP Screen Personas already provides a JavaScript-based scripting environment, and the ability to call released OData services significantly expands what can be achieved without changing the standard application.
