entry.title: Create OData Web API Service for standard Table using Generate ABAP Repository Objects wizard in ADT
entry.content:
Introduction:

In this Blog, I want to walk through the detailed steps to create OData Web API Service for a standard storage Bin table:/SCWM/LAGP with low-code/no-code.

The main idea is to expose a standard database table as an OData Web API Service using the ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP), the fastest and most automated approach is to use the Generate ABAP Repository Objects wizard in ABAP Development Tools (ADT).
 
This method automatically generates the entire RAP stack—including the CDS Data Definitions, Behavior Definitions, Service Definition, and Service Binding

Target Audience and prerequisites:

  • ABAP developers who are new to RAP
  • Basic knowledge of CDS Views and ABAP Development Tools (ADT)
  • System used: SAP S/4HANA (On-Premise)

    Step 1. Create an ABAP package.

    This ABAP package will contain all the artefacts related to the OData Web API Service.

    In ADT, go to the Project Explorer, right-click on the System Instance, and select New > ABAP Package from the context menu.

     Maintain the required information, then Click Next >

             

    Select a transport request and click Finish

     Add the package created: “ZEWM_RAP_ST_BIN_DATA” to the favorite packages, using select Favorite Packages > ADD Package from the context menu.

     The package adds Under Favorite Packages:

     

    Step 2. Add Standard table to the favorite objects

    (no need to add if the table is already available in the Favorite Objects, just search for it).

    Right-click on Favorite Objects and select Add Object from the context menu

    Search for standard table :/SCWM/LAGP and click OK


    The Table /SCWM/LAGP adds under Favorite Objects

     

    Step 3. Create your OData v4 based WEB API service with the built-in ADT generator.

    Right-click the standard database table /SCWM/LAGP under favorite objects and select Generate ABAP Repository Objects from the context menu.


    Select OData Web API Service and click Next >.


    Provide the ABAP Package and click Next >.

    Maintain the required information on the Configure Generator dialog to provide the name of your data model, Behavior, Service Definition etc. 

    and click Next > to generate them.

    Select a transport request and click Finish

    Go to the Project Explorer, select your package refresh it by pressing F5, and check all generated ABAP repository objects

    The service binding is not generated due to inactive service definition, The conversion errors in the entity LC_LAGP00 are the cause for the inactive service definition.

    In SAP RAP (ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model), OData services block most standard DDIC conversion exists including ALPHA routines because they can cause runtime and formatting errors. 

    To resolve this, use a custom CDS type cast in your Core Data Services (CDS) view. After removing the errors in CDS View, activate the service definition and create the service Binding,

    Right click the service definition ‘ZAPI_LAGP_O4’ and select New Service Binding. Provide the Service Binding details and click Next >

     


    Select a transport request and click Finish

    Select the service Binding and Activate it.

    Right Click the CDS view and Select data Preview to display the filled database entries

      

    Step 4. Publish the local service endpoint of your service binding

    Open your service binding ‘ZSB_API_LAGP_O4 and click Publish.

     A local publish failure for OData V4 service bindings in ADT typically stems from backend gateway synchronization gaps, transport/client restrictions or an ADT/BTP Trial environment regression bug. You can resolve this by manually publishing via SAP Gateway or switching protocols.

    In case of above error, click on the Menu button Run ABAP Development Object as ABAP Application in SAPGUI or press Alt+F8.

     Type /iwfnd/v4_admin as a search string and double-click on the entry /IWFND/V4_ADMIN (Transaction).

    Click the button Publish Service Groups to get a list of service groups that can be published

    Enter following values to search for the service group of your service and press the button Get Service Groups:

    • System Alias: LOCAL
    • Service Group ID: ZSB_API_LAGP_O4

       

      Select the entry ZSB_API_LAGP_O4 from the list and press the button: Publish Service Groups. ￼

       Confirm the success message and press Enter. The service will be published

        

      Once the service is published, we get the service URL.

      Add your SAP Host and Port (http://<host>:<port>) to the Service URL (/sap/opu/odata4/sap/zsb_api_lagp_o4/srvd_a2x/sap/zapi_lagp_o4/0001/) to test the URL.

       we can use the URL in below ways:

      1. Paste the URL into a tool like Postman or your web browser to view the service metadata or data feeds.

      2. Connect the URL to SAP Business Application Studio or SAP UI5 projects to build user interfaces.

      3. Use the URL in non-SAP software or custom apps that need your data.

       
       Conclusion:

      We learned how to create OData Web API Service using the Generate ABAP Repository Objects wizard in ABAP Development Tools (ADT) to generate the entire RAP stack i.e., CDS Data Definitions, Behavior Definitions, Service Definition, and Service Binding automatically.

entry.title: Extracting SAC Parent-Child Hierarchies into Databricks Using OData
entry.content:
Introduction

During our work with SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC), I needed to make a parent-child hierarchy available in Databricks for downstream Data Science and analytics use cases. I initially approached the SAC dimension as a standard master-data extraction, but found that the hierarchy relationships required additional fields and a hierarchy-specific OData entity to preserve the parent-child structure.

SAP Analytics Cloud models can contain parent-child hierarchies that are important for reporting, consolidation, and downstream analytics. However, extracting a hierarchy is different from extracting a normal dimension. A flat master-data extract provides the members and their attributes, while a parent-child hierarchy also requires the relationships between those members.

In this article, I will walk through the approach I used to extract a hierarchy from SAC using OData and transform it into an analytics-ready structure in Databricks.

1. Finding the Hierarchy Endpoint

For a standard SAC dimension, the master-data endpoint follows a pattern such as:

<DIMENSION>Master
 
For a dimension containing a hierarchy, SAC provides a hierarchy-enabled endpoint:

 

<DIMENSION>MasterWithHierarchy
 
For example:
DIM_COMPANY_CODEMasterWithHierarchy
 
The hierarchy-enabled endpoint exposes additional fields associated with the hierarchy:
<HIERARCHY>_PARENTID
<HIERARCHY>_PREVID
<HIERARCHY>_ORDERID
These fields provide the information required to reconstruct the hierarchy outside SAC.

2. Understanding the Hierarchy Fields

SAC Field

Purpose

PARENTID

Identifies the immediate parent of a member.

PREVID

Identifies the previous sibling.

ORDERID

Represents the ordering of members under the same parent.

For example, SAC might return data similar to:

ID

Description

PARENTID

PREVID

ORDERID

GROUP_A

Group A

  

1

COMP_01

Company 01

GROUP_A

 

1

COMP_02

Company 02

GROUP_A

COMP_01

2

GROUP_A
├── COMP_01
└── COMP_02

The important point is that SAC does not need to return a nested JSON tree. The parent-child relationships can be reconstructed from these relationship fields.

3. Extracting the Data Using Python

Once I identified the hierarchy-enabled entity, I used a standard OData request to retrieve the hierarchy data.

import requests

url = BASE_URL + "DIM_COMPANY_CODEMasterWithHierarchy"

response = requests.get(
    url,
    headers=headers,
    params={
        "$top": 10000000    },
    timeout=120)

response.raise_for_status()

rows = response.json().get("value", [])

print(f"Rows received: {len(rows):,}")
In a production implementation, authentication information and environment-specific URLs should be stored securely rather than being hard-coded in the application.

4. Transforming the SAC Response

The SAC response can then be converted into a simpler hierarchy structure for Databricks.

Databricks Column

Description

node_id

Current hierarchy member

node_description

Member description

parent_id

Immediate parent

previous_sibling_id

Previous sibling

hierarchy_order

Member ordering

hierarchy_id

Hierarchy identifier

hierarchy_level

Calculated hierarchy depth

For example:

node_id = COMP_02
parent_id = GROUP_A
previous_sibling_id = COMP_01
hierarchy_order = 2
This can be interpreted as:
GROUP_A
   │
   ├── COMP_01
   │
   └── COMP_02
This structure makes the hierarchy easier for downstream applications to understand without requiring them to directly interpret the SAC-specific field names.

5. Storing the Hierarchy in Databricks

After transformation, I stored the hierarchy as a Delta table in Databricks.

df.write \
    .format("delta") \
    .mode("overwrite") \
    .option("overwriteSchema", "true") \
    .saveAsTable("your_catalog.your_schema.company_hierarchy")
The resulting table can then be queried using SQL or consumed by downstream Data Science applications.

6. Validating the Hierarchy

 

After loading the hierarchy into Databricks, I validated the structure to make sure the parent-child relationships had been preserved correctly.

Some useful checks include:

  • Are all hierarchy members present?
  • Does every non-root member have a valid parent?
  • Are there orphan relationships?
  • Do previous siblings exist?
  • Do siblings belong to the same parent?
  • What is the maximum hierarchy depth?
  • How many root members exist?

The validation process can be represented as:

SAC
 │
 ▼
OData Extraction
 │
 ▼
Hierarchy Transformation
 │
 ▼
Structural Validation
 │
 ├── Parent validation
 ├── Sibling validation
 ├── Root validation
 └── Depth validation
 │
 ▼
Databricks Delta Table
This step is particularly useful because successfully receiving records from SAC does not necessarily guarantee that the hierarchy relationships have been reconstructed correctly.

7. Using the Hierarchy

 

Once the hierarchy was available in Databricks, it could be used by downstream applications to traverse parents, children, ancestors, and descendants.

For example:

GROUP_A
   │
   ├── REGION_01
   │      ├── COMPANY_01
   │      └── COMPANY_02
   │
   └── REGION_02
          └── COMPANY_03
A Data Science application can therefore determine which companies belong to a particular group by traversing the hierarchy rather than maintaining a manually created mapping.

Potential use cases include:

  • Consolidation analysis
  • Hierarchy-based filtering
  • Parent/child reporting
  • Data aggregation
  • Data Science pipelines
  • Semantic layers and AI/Genie use cases

8. Architecture

 

 

Conclusion

The key to extracting a parent-child hierarchy from SAP Analytics Cloud is to use the hierarchy-enabled MasterWithHierarchy OData entity rather than treating the dimension as a standard flat master-data extract.

The hierarchy relationship fields:

PARENTID
PREVID
ORDERID
provide the information needed to reconstruct the parent-child structure outside SAC.

By transforming these relationships into a structured Databricks table, the hierarchy becomes available for reporting, analytics, Data Science, and downstream AI applications.

The overall approach is:

Discover → Extract → Transform → Validate → Store → Consume

entry.title: Testing SAP RAP OData Service Using SAP Gateway Client
entry.content:
Introduction:

The ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) provides a modern framework for developing transactional applications and exposing business data through OData services. Once a RAP service is created and published using a Service Binding, it is important to test the exposed service and verify that the different operations work as expected.

In this blog, I will demonstrate how to test a SAP RAP OData Service using the SAP Gateway Client. The testing covers the service URL, entity set operations, CRUD operations, filtering, and RAP business validations and determination.

The service binding used in this example is:

ZSB_TE_MATERIAL_V

Service URL:

/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZSB_TE_MATERIAL_V

Entity Set:

zC_te_material_V

The following operations will be tested:

  • Reading a single record using key fields

  • Filtering records using $filter

  • Creating a new record using POST

  • Updating an existing record using PATCH

  • Deleting a record using DELETE

  • Testing RAP business validations

  • Handling validation errors in SAP Gateway Client

  • Verifying that invalid records are not created

  • Testing RAP determination to automatically calculate and update the Totalprice

 in service binding we will have service URL to testing in sap gateway.

GET Operation – Reading a Record

The GET operation is used to retrieve an existing record from the RAP OData V2 service. To read a specific record, we need to provide the values of the key fields in the service URL.

Service URL:

/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZSB_TE_MATERIAL_V/zC_te_material_V(Materialid='103',Orderid='3')

In this example, the record is retrieved using Materialid = 103 and Orderid = 3 as the key fields.

Filter in Read Operation

The GET method can also be used to retrieve records based on specific conditions by using the OData $filter query option.

HTTP Method: GET

Service URL:

/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZSB_TE_MATERIAL_V/zC_te_material_V?$filter=Materialid eq '103'

In this example, the $filter option is used to retrieve records where Materialid is equal to 103.

POST Operation – Creating a New Record

The POST operation is used to create a new record in the RAP OData V2 service. To create a record, the required field values are passed in the HTTP request body.

HTTP Method: POST

Service URL:

/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZSB_TE_MATERIAL_V/zC_te_material_V

HTTP Request Body:

{
  "Materialid": "104",
  "Orderid": "4",
  "Materialname": "LOGI Keyboard",
  "Price": "1600",
  "Quantity": "2",
  "Totalprice": "3200"
}

 

PATCH Operation – Updating an Existing Record

To update an existing record, the key field values must be provided in the request URL. The fields that need to be changed are passed in the HTTP request body.

The update is performed using the PATCH HTTP method.

Request URL:

/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZSB_TE_MATERIAL_V/zC_te_material_V(Materialid='101',Orderid='100')

HTTP Request Body:

{
  "Materialname": "Gaming Laptop",
  "Price": "2500",
  "Quantity": "3",
  "Totalprice": "7500"
}

In this example, the record identified by Materialid = 101 and Orderid = 100 is updated with the new material name, price, quantity, and total price.

Verifying the Updated Record

After successfully performing the update operation, we can use the GET method to retrieve the record again and verify that the changes have been applied successfully.

By using the same key fields in the request URL, we can confirm that the updated values are reflected in the response.

DELETE Operation

The DELETE method is used to delete an existing record by passing its key field values in the request URI.

Request URI:
/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZSB_TE_MATERIAL_V/zC_te_material_V(Materialid='101',Orderid='100')

HTTP Method: DELETE

A successful deletion returns 204 – No Content.

Validation

The RAP application has validations for Material ID, Order ID, and Material Name.

The validation was triggered successfully, and the invalid record was not created.

determination for calculating the total price. When the Price and Quantity values are provided or changed, the determination is triggered and calculates the value automatically 

  • Http method : post 
  •  Request url :  /sap/opu/odata/sap/ZSB_TE_MATERIAL_V/zC_te_material_V

  • HTTP Request Body:

    {
  "Materialid": "112",
  "Orderid": "4",
  "Materialname": "gui det keybord ",
  "Price": "800",
  "Quantity": "5",
  "Totalprice": ""
}

     

Conclusion

In this blog, we explored how to test a SAP RAP OData Service using the SAP Gateway Client. We covered the complete CRUD operations, including GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE, along with filtering and verification of updated records.

We also tested the RAP business validations and verified that invalid records are prevented from being created through the Gateway Client and RAP determination, which automatically calculates Totalprice based on Price and Quantity, and verified that the calculated value is updated correctly.

This provides a simple and practical approach to testing RAP OData services and validating their behavior before consuming them in applications such as SAP Fiori.

entry.title: Reconciling EC Loan Advance Installments with ECP Payroll Results Using ABAP OData Integration
entry.content:
Background

One of the more nuanced integration challenges in an SAP Employee Central Payroll (ECP) landscape is keeping SuccessFactors Employee Central (EC) in sync with what actually happened inside the payroll engine. This is especially true for loan advance management.
In EC, when a loan is approved for an employee, the system creates a structured repayment schedule — a set of installment records, each with a due date, an amount, and a status (NOT_PAID, PAID, PARTIALLY_PAID). EC holds the plan.
ECP, on the other hand, holds the reality. The actual salary deduction for the EMI happens inside the payroll run via specific wage types. EC has no automatic visibility into whether ECP deducted the right amount in a given month, or whether it deducted anything at all.
For this engagement, the client had multiple active loan types — for example, a car loan scheme, a marriage loan scheme, and an employee loan scheme. Each loan type had its own set of wage types covering issuance, regular recovery, off-cycle recovery, and outstanding balance. Someone on the payroll team was manually updating EC installment statuses every month after payroll closed. This PoC was built to eliminate that manual step entirely.

What We Built

We developed a custom ABAP report running inside ECP that does the following end to end:
  1. Reads each employee's installment schedule from EC via the AdvancesInstallments OData v2 API
  2. Reads the employee's complete payroll run history from the ECP payroll cluster
  3. Reconciles the two — did ECP actually deduct the EMI for each installment?
  4. Produces a comma-delimited CSV file formatted for EC's batch import job, updating each installment's status
  5. Displays results in an ALV grid for review before the file is uploaded
  6. Logs every step to SLG1 for audit purposes
No middleware. No integration platform. A single ABAP program running directly inside ECP, calling SuccessFactors over HTTP.

Solution Architecture

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   ECP (ABAP Stack)                  │
│                                                     │
│  Custom Report                                      │
│  ┌──────────────┐   OData GET   ┌─────────────────┐ │
│  │  OData       │ ────────────► │  SuccessFactors  │ │
│  │  Reader      │ ◄──────────── │  EC              │ │
│  │  (per PERNR) │   JSON resp.  │  AdvancesInst.   │ │
│  └──────────────┘               └─────────────────┘ │
│         │                                           │
│         ▼                                           │
│  ┌──────────────┐                                   │
│  │  Payroll     │  CU_READ_RGDIR + PYXX_READ        │
│  │  Cluster     │  PCL2 — complete run history      │
│  │  Reader      │                                   │
│  └──────────────┘                                   │
│         │                                           │
│         ▼                                           │
│  ┌──────────────┐                                   │
│  │ Reconcilia-  │  FIFO matching                    │
│  │ tion Engine  │  PAID / NOTPAID / EXCEPTION       │
│  └──────────────┘                                   │
│         │                                           │
│         ▼                                           │
│  ┌──────────────┐                                   │
│  │  CSV Writer  │  AL11 output → EC Batch Import    │
│  └──────────────┘                                   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The program is structured as an OO ABAP report — a local class hierarchy with clearly separated responsibilities:
 
Class Responsibility
lcl_loggerSLG1 application log wrapper
lcl_odata_readerHTTP call and JSON parsing for EC OData
lcl_cluster_readerPCL2 cluster read and off-cycle detection
lcl_wt_configWage type mapping (from custom config table)
lcl_reconcilerFIFO EMI matching logic
lcl_csv_writerEC upload file formatting and write
lcl_alv_displayALV result grid

The OData Integration — Key Technical Points

This is the part that had the most surprises, so it deserves the most detail.

Connection Setup

The HTTP connection to SuccessFactors is configured as an SM59 HTTP destination. Authentication is handled via OAuth 2.0 — the SM59 destination manages token acquisition automatically. The ABAP code uses cl_http_client=>create_by_destination to obtain an HTTP client object and issues a standard GET request. No custom token management code is needed inside the report itself.

The Entity and URL Structure

The OData entity being called is AdvancesInstallments. A typical request URL looks like this:
/odata/v2/AdvancesInstallments
  ?$filter=startswith(Advance_externalCode,'<PERNR>_')
  &$select=externalCode,Advance_externalCode,installmentAmount,
           installmentStatus,balanceRemaining,paymentDate,
           currencyGO,lastModifiedDateTime
  &$format=json
The Advance_externalCode field is the foreign key linking each installment back to its parent loan advance record. Its format typically includes the employee PERNR as a prefix, so filtering with startswith(Advance_externalCode,'<PERNR>_') returns all installments across all loan types for that employee in a single call.

The Critical SF OData v2 Limitation — One Call Per Employee

The most important gotcha in this integration: you cannot reliably combine multiple employees in a single OData call using OR filters on startswith.
The intuitive approach would be to build a combined filter like:
startswith(Advance_externalCode,'EMP001_') or
startswith(Advance_externalCode,'EMP002_') or
startswith(Advance_externalCode,'EMP003_')
In practice, SF OData v2 silently returns results for only the first condition and ignores the rest. No HTTP error is raised — you simply receive incomplete data with no indication that anything went wrong. That is far more dangerous than an outright error.
The solution is to make one dedicated HTTP GET call per employee PERNR. For a typical payroll run this is perfectly acceptable in terms of performance. For large employee populations, a pagination loop using $skip and $top should be added in a production implementation.

JSON Parsing

SF returns the response as a JSON structure where the d.results array contains one object per installment. Rather than relying on a full JSON library — which can have version dependencies across ECP landscapes — the report uses lightweight string parsing: locating known field name anchors and extracting the value between surrounding quotes or up to the next delimiter.
Dates come back in Microsoft OData /Date(milliseconds)/ format and are converted to ABAP DATS format by dividing the millisecond value by 86,400,000 and applying the standard Unix epoch offset.

Reading the ECP Payroll Cluster

The payroll cluster read has an important design decision worth explaining: there is no payroll period on the selection screen.
Instead of reading just one month's results, the report calls CU_READ_RGDIR to fetch the complete payroll run directory for each employee — every finalised run from the beginning of employment to the current date. It then loops through every directory entry and reads the RT (Results Table) for each run using PYXX_READ_PAYROLL_RESULT, specifying the country-specific cluster area via the MOLGA parameter.
The reason for reading the entire history rather than a single period is reconciliation completeness. To correctly determine whether an installment is PAID or NOTPAID, you need the full deduction history. An installment that was partially recovered in one month and topped up in the next requires both runs to be assessed correctly.

Off-Cycle Detection

Regular monthly runs and off-cycle runs (loan issuances, bonus runs, corrections) are handled differently. Off-cycle runs are identified by two checks combined with OR logic:
  • The SRTZA flag in the run directory entry is 'B'
  • The run's for-period begin date equals its for-period end date — a single-day period, which is characteristic of loan issuance off-cycle runs
Off-cycle deductions are logged but excluded from the installment matching, since they represent loan events rather than regular EMI recoveries.

The Reconciliation Logic

With the OData installments and the payroll RT entries both loaded for an employee, the reconciler works as follows:
  1. Groups the RT wage type entries by loan type using a custom configuration table
  2. For each loan type, sorts the EC installments by due date ascending — oldest first
  3. Applies a FIFO match — the oldest unreconciled installment is matched first against the available deduction amount
The outcome per installment:
 
Condition Status Written to CSV
Deduction ≥ 95% of installment amountPAID
Deduction > 0 but < 95%NOTPAID
No deduction foundNOTPAID
ECP has deduction but EC has no matching installmentEXCEPTION — separate file
The 95% threshold rather than 100% accounts for minor rounding differences that can arise in payroll calculations.

The EC Upload File — 12-Column Format

The CSV output follows the exact template that EC's Advance Installments batch import job accepts:
  • Row 1 — technical API field names as EC expects them
  • Row 2 — human-readable column labels
  • Row 3 onwards — one data row per installment
Two fields use the special EC token &&NO_OVERWRITE&&:
  • paymentDate — the report does not override whatever payment date EC already holds
  • amortization — EC retains its existing value
The amortizationTotal column is intentionally left blank — EC calculates this value itself.
EXCEPTION rows are written to a separate file so they can be reviewed manually before any action is taken in EC.

The Wage Type Mapping Table

Rather than hardcoding wage types inside the ABAP logic, the mapping is externalised into a custom SE11 transparent table. This makes the solution maintainable — adding a new loan type in future only requires a new table entry, not a code change and transport.
The table holds the country grouping (MOLGA), wage type, a description, and an active flag. The report reads this table dynamically at runtime, so the ABAP code itself contains no client-specific wage type values.

Key Learnings and Gotchas

Having built and iterated through this PoC, here are the things worth knowing before attempting something similar:
1. SF OData v2 OR filters on startswith are unreliable for multiple values. Always make one call per employee. Do not attempt to batch multiple employees in a single filter expression — you will get silently incomplete results.
2. /Date(ms)/ is the date format you will receive — plan to parse it. There is no automatic conversion. You need to handle the millisecond-to-ABAP-date arithmetic yourself.
3. CU_READ_RGDIR combined with PYXX_READ_PAYROLL_RESULT is the correct payroll cluster read path for ECP. Avoid direct PCL2 reads unless PYXX fails with a type conflict (return code 8), in which case consider the country-specific variant of the payroll result read function module.
4. Off-cycle detection using the SRTZA flag alone is not always sufficient. Add the FPBEG = FPEND single-day check as a fallback — some off-cycle run types in certain country versions do not set SRTZA correctly.
5. &&NO_OVERWRITE&& is essential in EC batch uploads. Use it for any field you do not intend to update. Without it, an empty CSV column will blank out the field in EC — which for a date or amount field can cause data corruption.
6. SLG1 logging is non-negotiable for payroll integrations. Every HTTP call, every employee processed, every exception — log it. Payroll disputes are always easier to resolve when you have a timestamped audit trail of exactly what the program read and decided.
 

Conclusion

The integration pattern described here — an ABAP OData consumer inside ECP reconciling against payroll cluster results — is broadly applicable beyond loan advances. Any scenario where EC holds a plan and ECP holds the execution reality follows the same structural pattern: arrears management, advance salary recoveries, third-party remittance reconciliation.
The key insight from this PoC is that ECP already has everything it needs to drive this reconciliation. The payroll cluster contains the ground truth on what was actually processed. SF OData provides structured, filterable access to the EC-side plan. Connecting the two in ABAP, with a proper class structure and audit log, produces a reliable and auditable automation with no dependency on a middleware platform.
Questions and comments welcome below.

entry.title: Software 3.0 - AI & Agentic Engineering for SAP Fiori and SAPUI5 Development
entry.content:
Agentic AI can now produce a working SAPUI5 application in hours rather than weeks.

The engineering question is no longer whether an agent can write the code, but how a Fiori development team keeps that speed inside enterprise design, data and release discipline. 

 A recent SAP Community article, “How to use the new Google IDE Antigravity with SAP (and CAP)”, provides a useful prelude to this discussion. It shows how an agent-first development environment can be connected to the SAP ecosystem: install Node.js and the development kit, configure SAP extensions, and expose project context through an MCP server. 

The toolchain used throughout this walkthrough: SAPUI5 in Google AntiGravity. 

But installing an agentic IDE is only the beginning. The more important question is this: what does it mean, to engineer a production-grade SAP Fiori application when agents such as Claude and Gemini can already generate a full SAPUI5 application that follows SAP Fiori design guidelines and best practices? These agents no longer stop at generation. They inspect the repository, edit several files at once, run the application against mock data, observe failures and revise their own work.

The definition of development work is changing. 

This article sets out a step-by-step path for using agentic coding to build SAPUI5 applications. The method is not theoretical — it has produced thousands of lines of code across several SAPUI5 Fiori applications, running in production. Each step is illustrated with numbered screenshots from that work, so the method can be verified. 

By the end of this article you will be able to scaffold a SAPUI5 project with SAP Fiori tools, brief an agent against the SAP Fiori Design Guidelines, validate the screen with mock data, map every binding to OData metadata, prove the application under realistic system load, and release it through a governed transport.

 

Software 3.0 changes the Fiori software development lifecycle at its core.

In the agentic era, the Fiori expert defines the experience and the guardrails, uses SAP Fiori tools to establish the project correctly, and treats an AI agent such as Google Antigravity or Claude Code as an implementation partner that can plan, edit, run, inspect and refine the application. This article follows that workflow in Google Antigravity, which Google describes as an “agent-first development platform” where agents plan, execute and verify complex work across the editor, terminal and browser, and where tangible artifacts such as implementation plans, browser controls and screenshots make the work easy for a human to verify.

The Core idea is to have production-ready SAPUI5 Fiori application, moving through six controlled stages: scaffold, prompt, simulate, map, load-test, and release.

The working model is simple. Start with SAP Fiori Guided Development, let the agent generate and refine the UI, and validate it with mock data. Map every binding against the OData metadata and the underlying Virtual Data Model (VDM), the CDS-based model that an S/4HANA service exposes. Then prove the application under realistic system load before moving it to production.

This makes Software 3.0 tangible for Fiori: the human defines the business outcome, architecture and guardrails, while the agent performs the fast paced implementation, testing, debugging and iteration.

 

A. From Software 1.0 to Software 3.0

A useful way to think about the evolution is to ask how the developer programs in today's era. 

 

Era

Primary programming mechanism

Developer focus

Software 1.0

Hand-written code

Statements, functions, algorithms

Software 2.0

Auto-complete, Code generation, Pair Programming

Data, objective, logic.

Software 3.0 (Since early 2026 onwards)

Natural-language instructions + AI agents

Context, architecture, constraints, verification

 

New Development Plan: Requirement -> Architect -> Agent Plan -> Multi-file Implementation -> Diff Checks -> Runtime Verification -> Agentic PRs/ Release

The result is a different development loop. Instead of write, run, debug and repeat, the cycle becomes state the intent, review the agent's plan, let it implement across files, then check diffs and the runtime evidence it returns. The developer's time moves from typing the change to judging whether the change is right.

 

B. The Six-Step Agentic Fiori Method

The Agentic UI5 development model deliberately separates Fiori element design, frontend implementation, system testing, and production governance. That separation is what prevents a fast prototype from becoming an ungoverned production change.

 

Stage

Human owns

Agent accelerates

Evidence before moving on

1. Create the foundation

App scope, Fiori floorplan, service target

Project files, manifests, initial views

A runnable Freestyle project with a clear file structure

2. Prompt the UI5 implementation

Fiori Design Guidelines, responsive behaviour, naming rules

Multi-file XML/JS/i18n/CSS changes and refactoring, logic builds

Diff review, design checklist, and a working local preview

3. Test with mock data

Scenarios, edge cases, expected states

Mock data generation, loading states, error cases

Repeatable local tests with metadata-accurate responses

4. Map XML OData metadata

VDM/service semantics, key fields, associations, business rules

Entity-to-control mapping and binding scaffolding

A mapping table, validated bindings

5. Move into SAP Business Application Studio for full-system testing

Test scope, destinations, authorizations, performance thresholds

Test harnesses, scripts, diagnostics, and remediation proposals

System-level test results and resolved defects

6. Implement in production

Approval, security, transport, rollout, support

Build checks, release notes, deployment assistance

Approved artifact deployed to Production via the Transport and App visible through the intended launchpad path

 

 

C. Walkthrough: the six steps in practice

Before working through the six steps, lets put the baseline in place. You need Node.js with the UI5 tooling; SAP Fiori tools (Application Wizard, Guided Development and Service Modeler) in Visual Studio Code or SAP Business Application Studio; an agentic IDE such as Google Antigravity; a development OData service, or a saved copy of its $metadata document; and a destination or transport path to the target system. Every step below assumes this baseline exists. 

Figure 1. SAP UI5  tools in NPM package

 

1. Create a Freestyle Fiori application with Fiori Guided Development

Start with the SAP-aware foundation instead of asking an agent to invent a UI5 project structure. SAP Fiori tools in Visual Studio Code gives you three things you need in sequence: an Application Wizard that generates both SAP Fiori elements and freestyle SAPUI5 templates, Guided Development that applies supported how-to guidance for adding functionality, and a Service Modeler that lets you inspect the OData metadata behind the service, including entities, properties and associations. This matters because the wizard produces the layout, manifest and build configuration that SAP itself supports, so the agent works inside a structure the platform can run, test and deploy.

The accurate working pattern is therefore: use the Application Wizard to create the Freestyle SAPUI5 project, then use Guided Development and the Fiori Tools modelers to establish supported patterns.

The initial project should contain a predictable structure: manifest.json, Component.js, XML views, controllers, fragments, i18n resources, models, test folders, and a localService area for mock assets.

·      SAP Fiori Tools

 

·      SAP Fiori Generator

 

 

·      Template Selection: Use Upload a Metadata Document

Figure 2. Guided Development in SAP Fiori tools: the supported how-to guide selected for this application, and the generated code step it applies to the project.

 

·      Running through the option in Guided Development: The complexity increases - Then it is time to invoke the Agents.

 

Figure 3. Guided Development in SAP Fiori tools and AI Agents: the supported how-to guide selected for this application, and the generated code step it applies to the project.

 

·      Final Base SAP Fiori UI5 Program Structure

 

Figure 4. The base freestyle SAPUI5 project generated by the SAP Fiori tools Application Wizard, showing manifest.json, Component.js, XML views, controllers, fragments, i18n resources, models, test folders and the localService area for mock assets.

 

2. Prompt the UI5 implementation against SAP Fiori Design Guidelines

Open the generated codebase in the agentic IDE ie Google Antigravity. Now-forth, we will use Natural language for Prompting and will bring  the required features to existence. The quality of an agentic result depends on the quality of the context you give it. Do not prompt with “build me a dashboard.” Give Antigravity a structured brief: the business task and the persona it serves,  the entity sets and fields to bind, the files it may touch, the conventions it must obey, and the checks that must pass before it reports back.

This is where SAP Fiori expertise matters most. The agent should be instructed to preserve responsive behavior, clear information hierarchy, meaningful empty and busy states, content density, internationalization and semantic status colors. It should also understand that XML views, controllers, formatters, manifest.json, and i18n.properties form one coordinated change rather than six unrelated files. This is where the "TASTE" of the developer/Functional Profession matters in designing the UX.

 

·      Prompting and Agent Capability Examples

The screenshots that follow run through two agents: Codex and Google Antigravity. They are included as documentary evidence of the overall Agent engineering features described above - the brief, the implementation plan, the multi-file diff, the run against mock data, and the correction that followed - rather than as a comparison of the two products.

·      Codex Agent

Figure 5. A Codex session on the same repository: the task brief given to the agent, the files it selected to change, and the implementation it proposed before any code was written to disk.

 

·      Anti-Gravity Agentic Development IDE

In Google Antigravity, heavily rely on /grill-me mode to clarify that the Agent has understood the Feature requirements correctly before proceeding. This is the most important as "Tokens" are as good as "Cash" these days. !

Figure 6. The Google Antigravity agent harness: the implementation plan produced before any file is changed, alongside the editor, terminal and browser surfaces the agent works across.

 

·      Code Diff checks

Figure 7. The multi-file diff returned by the agent, covering the XML view, controller, manifest.json and i18n resources as one coordinated change rather than four unrelated edits.

 

 

·      Code Performance review by Agents

Figure 8. An agent-run performance review of the UI5 implementation, listing the issues found in the generated code and the correction proposed for each.

 

 

·      UI5 Fiori Elements logic implementation

 

Figure 9. SAP Fiori elements logic implemented by the agent, showing how the described business task was turned into a working view and controller.

 

·      Fiori Elements – Few Examples created by Agents

 

·      Inverted Status

 

·      Progress Line Bar Inline Graph

 

·      Delta Graph%

 

·      Harvey Inline Micro-chart

Figure 10. The generated SAP Fiori elements screens rendered in the running application, showing the floorplan, list behaviour and semantic status colours prescribed in the brief.

 

·      Fiori Application Errors during development - Solved by AI Agents

Figure 11. Errors raised by the Fiori application during development, captured from the console and network output that the agent uses as the input to its debugging loop.

 

·      Anti-Gravity Browser based Automated Testing Loop for Agentic Debugging of Errors

The Most Important features of Google Antigravity is the /goal Mode and the Browser based Self- Testing.

 

Figure 12. The Antigravity browser-based test loop: the agent runs the application, reads the browser and network output, revises the code and repeats until the scenario passes, returning the run as a reviewable artifact.

 

·      Software Debugging – Agentic Workflow for Root cause Analysis

Figure 13. The agentic root-cause analysis workflow, tracing a failure from the symptom observed in the browser back to the responsible binding and the code change that introduced it.

 

The operating rule is plan first, edit second, verify continuously. Ask the agent to produce an implementation plan before it changes files. Review the plan for scope and architecture. Then let it make a small, coherent change, run the local application, inspect console and browser output. A short cycle is safer than one enormous prompt that changes the entire repository.

 

3. Test with a mock-data generator

A Fiori screen should become testable before it depends on a live SAP backend.  A Mock Server simulates a backend from local service metadata and mock data, allowing developers to test without depending on the availability of the real service or adding load to the system where the service runs. 

Use the mock stage to generate synthetic data that mirrors the shape of production: full result sets and empty ones, long texts and null values, boundary dates, large numbers, every status value the UI colour-codes. 

 

Figure 14. Mock data generated from the service metadata and served by the SAPUI5 Mock Server, covering full result sets, empty results, long texts, null values, boundary dates and every status value the UI colour-codes.

Prompt Antigravity to add or vary data one scenario at a time. Then ask it to run the mock page, capture the rendered result and report what each scenario proves. This turns mock data into a repeatable visual regression check you can run again after every change.

 

4. Use XML OData metadata for VDM and OData mapping logic

The XML document available at the service’s /$metadata endpoint is useful. It is not a substitute for domain knowledge, but it is the reliable starting point for the Agent to mapp the frontend to the backend. For SAP S/4HANA scenarios, the service may represent data from a CDS-based Virtual Data Model. The frontend agent must consume what the service actually exposes.

Figure 15. The OData $metadata document inspected in the SAP Fiori tools Service Modeler, showing the entity sets, keys, properties, associations and annotations used to validate every binding in the application.

 

·      SAPUI5 Fiori UI/UX Experience- Created by SAPUI5 AI Agentic Engineering

  • UX - STAGE 1 (Initial Prompting)

 

  •  UX - FINAL STAGE (Multiple Rounds of Prompting)

Figure 16. A sample snip of a SAPUI5 Fiori application A Custom Project Management Dashboard with Agentic Development

 

·      KPIs Tiles – Created by SAPUI5 Agentic Engineering

Note that 

·      Sample Purchase Order Overview Dashboard with superior UI/UX – Created by SAPUI5 AI Agentic Engineering

Figure 17. Sample KPIs and SAPUI5 Fiori Applications created in Google AntiGravity with agentic engineering, rendered in the finished application with superior UI/UX (Represented here with Anonymised Mock Data only)

Note that till that we are operating in Local Development, only.

 

5. Move the application into SAP Business Application Studio for full-system, authorization and load testing

The fifth step moves the application from a local, metadata-driven prototype into an environment where its end-to-end assumptions can be tested. SAP Business Application Studio is an appropriate development and deployment environment for SAP Fiori projects.

The practical sequence is:

  • Import or clone the UI5 project into SAP BAS and confirm that the generated project runs without the local-only assumptions hidden by the prototype.
  • Run functional tests, including authorization failures, empty results, long-running reads, paging, optimistic concurrency, and backend errors.
  • Run performance and load tests at the system boundary. Measure browser rendering, request latency, payload size, Gateway and backend resource consumption. Do not treat a local mock test as a load test.

 

6. Implement in production

Production implementation is a governed release. Before release, the team should confirm that the build is reproducible, unit and integration tests have passed, the app meets accessibility and responsive requirements,  security and authorization behaviour is understood and the target SAPUI5/runtime version is compatible.

·      Preparing for Production

Figure 18. Production readiness evidence: build, test and configuration checks collected and reviewed before the change was submitted for release approval.

The final production checklist should cover the target deployment landscape, package and transport details, destination and authentication configuration, versioning, launchpad intent and role assignment, monitoring, rollback, and support ownership. The agent can prepare release notes, documentation, deployment checklists, and test evidence. 

 

Agent SKILLS: fiori_SKILLS.md

There is a major difference between "Let an AI build my Fiori app" and "Let an engineering agent build my Fiori app according to my enterprise architecture." The difference is context.

fiori_SKILLS.md is a production-oriented knowledge base and operating manual for AI coding agents working on SAP Fiori and SAPUI5 code. The Fiori_SKILLS.md captures what an agent cannot infer from the code alone:

  • Identity — application metadata, namespaces, OData services and entity mappings.
  • Structure — the UI model, the frontend architecture, and the files an agent may and may not modify.
  • Craft — coding conventions, reusable implementation playbooks, and the anti-patterns already ruled out on this project.
  • Proof — testing standards, performance constraints and the deployment rules a change must satisfy before release.

fiori_SKILLS.md carries the project architecture, naming conventions, accepted patterns, performance limits and safe modification boundaries into every agent session, so the same rules apply on the hundredth prompt as on the first. Without it, each session starts again from generic training knowledge and the guardrails have to be retyped by hand.

 

D. The operating model: Architect,  System & Agent 

Agentic development works when responsibilities are explicit. The SAP Fiori expert owns user experience, enterprise constraints, data semantics, architectural trade-offs, and release decisions. Google Antigravity coordinates implementation work across the editor, terminal, and browser and produces reviewable artifacts. SAP tooling and the target system provide the supported project model, service contract, runtime behaviour, authorization boundaries, deployment process, and production evidence.

Responsibility

Human architect/developer

Agentic AI

SAP platform/tooling

Experience

Define persona, task, hierarchy, and Fiori pattern

Generate candidate XML and styling changes

Provide supported controls and design-system behaviour

Code

Review diffs and approve architecture

Edit related files, refactor, and test locally

Build and run the UI5 project

Data

Interpret VDM/service semantics and business rules

Inventory metadata and propose bindings

Expose OData metadata, annotations, and responses

Quality

Set acceptance criteria and approve evidence

Run repeatable checks and explain failures

Provide mock server, test, destination, and environment capabilities

Release

Approve change, security, transport, and rollout

Prepare artifacts and release notes

Deploy and integrate with launchpad/runtime

The discipline: Never allow - speed of the Agent to outrun evidence in the browser or the deployment pipeline.

 

E.  Conclusion: Teach the AI Agent "The Method", Not Just the Prompt

Google Antigravity provides an environment in which the AI agent can plan, edit, execute and verify. SAP Fiori Guided Development provides the initial application structure. XML OData metadata and VDM information provide authoritative backend context. Mock data provides a fast feedback loop. BAS backed testing provides the bridge to realistic system validation.

 

Figure 19. A list of AI Agents available in Google Antigravity, which can be leveraged for SAP Fiori UI5 Agentic Coding. The models are getting more powerful with each passing week.

 

Software 3.0 pattern for SAPUI5 Fiori Development:

-- " Teach the agent the architecture, give it the right system context, verify diffs and every result against browser load evidence, rather than against the prompt..."

The practical promise of agentic engineering in the SAP Fiori world: from “Months” of manual efforts to  “only to a Few Weeks” of Human supervised, AI-Agent driven work.

 

The Future is the Agentic Way...! 🤖🤖
