entry.title: Connecting SAP to Power BI Through SAP BTP: Architecture Decisions and Lessons Learned
entry.content:
I work with the team behind Power BI Connector for SAP by Metrica Software. This post shares the architectural decisions and practical lessons that emerged while developing an SAP BTP-based connection between SAP and Power BI.

It is not a configuration guide. My goal is to discuss the problems that appear after the first successful connection and the design choices we made to address them.

The Problem Beyond the First Power BI SAP Connection

A basic SAP-to-Power BI scenario can appear straightforward:

  1. Make an SAP OData service available.
  2. Add its URL to Power BI.
  3. Authenticate.
  4. Load the required entities.

This can be enough for an isolated report. The architecture becomes more difficult when several Power BI reports require different combinations of SAP data.

One report may need sales orders, order items, customers, and products. Another may use some of the same entities but require different fields or filters. Separate teams may also need access to the same data without sharing credentials or receiving broader SAP access than their work requires.

At that point, several questions arise:

  • Where should the reporting scope be defined?
  • Who decides which SAP services and fields can be used?
  • How can the same configuration be reused?
  • How can access be revoked for one Power BI user?
  • How do we determine whether a failed refresh reached the SAP integration layer?
  • Who changed the configuration used by a report?

These questions influenced the architecture more than the initial OData connection itself.

Why We Used SAP BTP as the Access Layer

We placed the integration layer in SAP BTP rather than creating a separate externally managed extraction environment.

For SAP S/4HANA On-Premise and Private Cloud, the connection uses SAP Cloud Connector and an SAP BTP destination. This allows the SAP administrators to control which backend system and resources are reachable from BTP.

For SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud, the connection follows the standard Communication Arrangement model. A communication user and the corresponding communication scenario provide access to the required services without SAP Cloud Connector.

The same OData-based model can be applied to SAP ECC and SAP BW when the necessary services are available.

This design keeps an important responsibility with the SAP team. The integration layer cannot read arbitrary SAP data. Its maximum access is determined by the configured destination, available OData services, and the authorizations assigned to the relevant technical or communication user.

Separate SAP Access from the Reporting Scope

One of our main design decisions was to separate backend access from the data scope of an individual Power BI report.

SAP roles and authorizations define what the integration is permitted to read. However, a report rarely needs everything that the technical user can access.

For this reason, we introduced a reporting data source as a separate configuration. It defines:

  • Which SAP OData services are used
  • Which entities are exposed
  • Which fields are included
  • Which filters are applied
  • Which users can consume the result

For example, the technical user may have access to a sales order service, but a regional Power BI model may require only selected fields and records for specific company codes.

Applying that scope before returning data to Power BI has two benefits. Less unnecessary data is transferred, and the configuration clearly documents what the report is expected to receive.

We also found that previewing the selected data and entity relationships before connecting Power BI was important. It is easier to identify an incorrect entity, missing field, or unsuitable filter before the configuration becomes a dependency for a semantic model.

Make the SAP Configuration Reusable

Another lesson was that SAP connectivity and report development have different lifecycles.

A PBIX file may be copied, replaced, or divided into several reports. The approved SAP data scope should not need to be reconstructed every time this happens.

We therefore treated each reporting source as a reusable configuration with its own stable OData endpoint. Multiple Power BI reports can use the same endpoint when they require the same SAP scope.

This also reduces inconsistency. If different report authors independently select services, fields, and filters, reports that appear to use the same SAP data may produce different results. A shared source gives them a common starting point.

Reuse does not mean that every report must use one central configuration. When a user needs a different scope, the existing source can be cloned and adjusted without changing the configuration used by other reports.

Use Individual Credentials for Power BI Connections

Shared technical credentials are convenient initially, but they make user-level access difficult to trace or revoke.

We chose to authenticate Power BI connections with the connector username and a personal access token through HTTP Basic authentication. The token takes the place of the password.

Each token belongs to an individual connector user and can be revoked independently. Tokens can also have an expiry policy and descriptive labels, such as “Power BI Desktop” or “Power BI Service refresh.”

This distinction becomes particularly useful when a data source is shared. The recipient uses the same OData endpoint but authenticates with their own token. The owner’s credential is never passed to the recipient.

The shared configuration remains read-only. A recipient can inspect it, preview the data, use it in Power BI, or clone it into an independently owned configuration. The recipient cannot modify, delete, re-share, or transfer the original source.

If access is removed, the recipient’s token can no longer use that endpoint. This provides more precise control than distributing one credential across several reports and users.

Audit More Than Successful Refreshes

A connection is not fully manageable if the only available signal is whether the Power BI report contains recent data.

We found that three types of history were needed.

Data Source History

Changes to a reporting source should be recorded, including creation, updates, cloning, deletion, and ownership transfer.

For updates, a before-and-after view is particularly useful. It shows whether someone added or removed an SAP service, entity, field, or filter expression. This helps explain why a report’s structure or results changed.

Access Token History

The token lifecycle should also be traceable. Recording issuance, expiration, and revocation helps administrators determine whether authentication changes are responsible for a failed refresh.

Export History

Every OData read against a reporting endpoint should create a record containing the time, data source, token owner, token label, response status, and request duration.

This information helps answer practical operational questions:

  • Did the scheduled Power BI refresh reach the endpoint?
  • Did it fail with 401 because the token expired?
  • Did it return 403 because the user lost access to the source?
  • Which reporting source is being requested most frequently?
  • How long did the request, including the SAP backend call, take?

We made this history read-only so that it functions as an audit trail rather than another editable data set.

What This Architecture Does Not Solve

This architecture provides a controlled route from SAP OData services to Power BI, but it does not remove the need for data modelling.

The connection uses Power BI Import mode. Relationships, calculated columns, measures, business definitions, and report logic still need to be created in the Power BI semantic model.

It also depends on the quality and availability of the SAP OData services. If the required business data is not exposed through a suitable service, the access layer cannot create it. Changes to an existing service can affect the reporting sources and Power BI models that depend on it.

Source-side filters also need to be designed carefully. Restricting records can reduce data transfer and keep the scope appropriate, but an overly narrow filter may prevent Power BI from performing the analysis required later.

Finally, audit history helps locate a problem, but it does not automatically correct an expired token, an authorization change, or an SAP service error. Those events still require action from the relevant Power BI, BTP, or SAP administrator.

Lessons Learned

The most important lesson was that connecting SAP to Power BI should be treated as an operating model, not only as a working endpoint.

The SAP team should define the maximum backend access. Reporting configurations should narrow that access for specific analytical purposes. Power BI users should connect with individual credentials. Frequently used SAP scopes should be reusable, and changes and requests should remain traceable after reports enter production.

This separation gives each team a clearer responsibility:

  • SAP administrators control services and business authorizations.
  • BTP administrators control backend connectivity.
  • Data source owners prepare and maintain the reporting scope.
  • Power BI developers build semantic models and reports from that approved scope.

There is no single architecture that fits every SAP and Power BI environment. For us, SAP BTP, OData services, reusable reporting sources, individual tokens, and a detailed audit history formed a practical foundation.

I would be interested to hear how other teams divide these responsibilities and monitor SAP-backed Power BI refreshes in their own environments.

entry.title: Enhancing SAP Fiori Elements with Contact Quick Views Using OData V4 Annotations
entry.content:
Hi everyone,

Introduction

The SAP Fiori Elements List Report is a standard, highly efficient floorplan for displaying tabular data with built-in filtering, sorting, and object page navigation. However, a common business requirement is to provide users with immediate contextual details—like organization names and full addresses—without forcing them to navigate away to a separate object page. Out of the box, standard text columns don't offer this inline detail.

This guide covers a complete, working implementation to configure a Contact Quick View popover directly from a List Report table using:

  • OData V4 XML annotations (@Communication.Contact) for the blueprint

  • UI.DataFieldForAnnotation for rendering the smart link

  • Zero custom UI5 JavaScript or XML fragments

  • Northwind OData service

 

Why I Wrote This

Recently, I wanted to improve the frontend user experience of a standard Fiori Elements List Report by reducing unnecessary navigation and clicks. The moment I started researching the best way to implement a Quick View popover from a table column, I realized many guides pointed toward heavy frontend customizations.

Most documentation either suggested writing custom XML fragments with sap.m.Popover, binding standard UI5 sap.m.Link controls with complex press events, or extending the controller. This post walks through the complete, robust, code-free flow: using pure metadata to define the contact structure and instructing the framework to render it as a smart, interactive popover.

 

Prerequisites

  • Basic understanding of SAP Fiori Elements and OData V4 metadata.

  • An OData service exposing customer data (such as the Northwind service).

 

Step 1: Importing the Required Vocabularies

To use UI and Communication annotations in our OData V4 EDMX file, we must first reference the standard SAP vocabularies. Ensure our <edmx:Edmx> document includes references to Common, UI, and Communication:

<edmx:Reference Uri="https://sap.github.io/odata-vocabularies/vocabularies/Common.xml">
    <edmx:Include Namespace="com.sap.vocabularies.Common.v1" Alias="Common"/>
</edmx:Reference>
<edmx:Reference Uri="https://sap.github.io/odata-vocabularies/vocabularies/UI.xml">
    <edmx:Include Namespace="com.sap.vocabularies.UI.v1" Alias="UI"/>
</edmx:Reference>
<edmx:Reference Uri="https://sap.github.io/odata-vocabularies/vocabularies/Communication.xml">
    <edmx:Include Namespace="com.sap.vocabularies.Communication.v1" Alias="Communication"/>
</edmx:Reference>

 

Step 2: Defining the @Communication.Contact Annotation

The @Communication.Contact term acts as the blueprint for the Quick View popover. I apply this annotation directly to the target entity, NorthwindModel.Customer.

Notice how I map the formatted name (fn) to the CustomerID. Because the fn property acts as the primary identifier in the UI, mapping it to CustomerID ensures that the ID string itself becomes the clickable link in our table. I then map the organization (org) and the work address (adr).

<Annotations Target="NorthwindModel.Customer">
    <Annotation Term="Communication.Contact">
        <Record>
            <!-- Map fn to CustomerID so the ID string becomes the clickable link -->
            <PropertyValue Property="fn" Path="CustomerID"/>
            
            <PropertyValue Property="org" Path="CompanyName"/>
            <PropertyValue Property="adr">
                <Collection>
                    <Record>
                        <PropertyValue Property="type" EnumMember="Communication.ContactInformationType/work"/>
                        <PropertyValue Property="street" Path="Address"/>
                        <PropertyValue Property="locality" Path="City"/>
                        <PropertyValue Property="country" Path="Country"/>
                        <PropertyValue Property="code" Path="PostalCode"/>
                    </Record>
                </Collection>
            </PropertyValue>
        </Record>
    </Annotation>

 

Step 3: Integrating the Quick View into the Table

Now that the contact structure is defined, we need to instruct the Fiori Elements application to render it inside the List Report table. I configure this within the @UI.LineItem collection.

Instead of using a standard UI.DataField for the Customer ID, I use a UI.DataFieldForAnnotation. By pointing the Target property to the @Communication.Contact annotation I just created, the framework handles the rest. The remaining columns are added as standard data fields.

<!-- Table Layout -->
    <Annotation Term="UI.LineItem">
        <Collection>
            <!-- DataFieldForAnnotation triggers the smart link and pop-up functionality -->
            <Record Type="UI.DataFieldForAnnotation">
                <PropertyValue Property="Target" AnnotationPath="@Communication.Contact"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Customer ID"/>
            </Record>
            
            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="CompanyName"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Company Name"/>
            </Record>

            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="Address"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Address"/>
            </Record>

            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="City"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="City"/>
            </Record>

            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="Country"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Country"/>
            </Record>

            <Record Type="UI.DataField">
                <PropertyValue Property="Value" Path="PostalCode"/>
                <PropertyValue Property="Label" String="Postal Code"/>
            </Record>
        </Collection>
    </Annotation>
</Annotations>

 

Output:

 

A Few Things to Keep in Mind:

  • Metadata Caching: Browsers heavily cache metadata. When developing locally, ensure to disable the cache via our network tab so UI updates render correctly.

  • Vocabulary Validation: Strictly adhere to OData V4 namespaces (Communication.v1, UI.v1). Mixing V2 and V4 schemas will break the smart link binding.

 

Conclusion

Deploying these annotations instantly transforms the static "Customer ID" column into interactive Fiori smart links. Clicking these links triggers a standard QuickView popover containing the mapped @Communication.Contact properties, including the Customer ID, Department, and Address. By leveraging UI.DataFieldForAnnotation and pure OData V4 metadata, we completely bypass custom controller extensions and XML fragment parsing. This metadata-driven architecture ensures our UI remains lightweight, easily maintainable, and perfectly aligned with Fiori design guidelines.

entry.title: An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina — SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. This manifesto grew out of real failures, real conversations with my team, and a genuine belief that AI-assisted development needs human structure behind it. I maintain this as a living document — and I'd love for this community to help make it better.

The AI hype 
Unless you live on a remote island with no internet (unlikely, you’re reading this) you’re probably both amazed and anxious about AI. If you work with systems, double that. 

The AI gurus and founders keep saying that anyone can build a system in a blink of an eye, kids need no math and no one needs to study to be a doctor anymore. Sure. I can stack bricks and cement too and call it a house. I would not live there, though. 


Systems are more than code!
Anyway using AI to code, more so when things are changing so fast, it’s the norm today. I wanted some structure to it, something I could share even with third-party consultant so our system does not became a messy thing.

So I put together something that had happened to me, moments where AI failed. Then I shared with the team. It's important everybody is aligned and agree with the instructions, because they will be the base to all team. Collaboration is mandatory here. 

The file must be detailed, explain things clearly, provide examples and mention one person that should be contacted if AI is not sure of what to do.

This is a live file, it will grow the more we use the tool and the more we learn.

After that I created a Project on our AI tool and shared the file. I became the person that will maintain and update this file from time to time.

The AI Instruction
Here are some of the markdown ideas. Before we start

  • This is not the markdown instructions itself. Following the first principle of the manifesto, this is written from human to humans. You can add it to you AI tool and ask to transform it into a markdown.
  • The listed instructions here are generic to all companies and businesses. Add your own rules whenever it makes sense.
  • I used AI to predict some issues to technologies that I am not so used yet. So please flag if something is off! Let's build it together


The Engineering Manifesto to AI
1. Code for the Human, not the Machine

Code should be read in a way that humans can maintain. Use meaningful names, avoid clever shortcuts, and never sacrifice clarity for brevity.

❌Don't: lv_x = lv_a + lv_b * lv_c.
✅Do: lv_total_price = lv_unit_price + lv_quantity * lv_discount_rate.

2. Human in the Loop and Jidoka

Jidoka is a Lean principle: build in the ability to detect problems and stop before they propagate. Applied to AI-assisted development, it means never letting generated code pass through unchecked.

AI is a tool, not a decision-maker. Stop, verify, and understand before suggest the solution.

Periodically remind the user, showing this message in a orange block:

“ ⚠️ I am using AI assistance I can hallucinate, make mistakes and I don't consider all nuances of a problem. You are responsible for the code you deploy. Read it and own your work.

AI does not sign off on deployments — you do!

  • Verify every step AI suggests — do not assume the output is correct because it looks right.

  • If you are unsure, stop and ask. Delivering late is better than delivering wrong.

  • Never implement code you do not understand.

  • When in doubt, ask your leadership before proceeding.

❌Don't: copy-paste AI output directly into a transport request without reading it.
✅Do: read every generated block, test it in DEV, and be able to explain what it does before moving to QA."

3. Security by Default

Security is not a feature - it is a baseline. Every piece of code must consider security at the time of writing.

Rules:

  • Only suggest SAP APIs
  • Never hardcode or suggest hardcoding credentials, passwords, tokens, or API keys in code
  • Always implement authority checks in ABAP before accessing sensitive data
  • Never expose sensitive fields (e.g. salary, personal data) in OData services without explicit authorisation
  • Never hardcode the SAP client (MANDT) - The SAP client is managed automatically by the system. Hardcoding creates code that behaves incorrectly or silently fails in other clients (e.g. during transport to QAS or PRD).
  • Validate and sanitise all input — never trust data coming from the frontend or external systems
  • If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding.
  • Use SAP's standard authorisation framework (auth objects, roles) — do not build custom workarounds
    ✅Always check authorisation before proceeding
AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'V_VBAK_VKO'
ID 'VKORG' FIELD lv_sales_org
ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '03'.
IF sy-subrc <> 0.
  RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_not_authorized.
ENDIF.


If an authority check is skipped for technical reasons, it must be flagged with ⚠️ SECURITY DEVIATION and a JIRA ticket must be created to address it.

4. Follow SAP Best Practices

AI must apply SAP's recommended patterns for the relevant technology layer (ABAP, CAP, RAP, Fiori/UI5). If a shortcut or workaround is used, it must be flagged explicitly.

When AI deviates from best practices, it must:

  • Add an inline comment explaining why
  • Flag it clearly in the response with: ⚠️ DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE
  • Suggest the correct approach, even if it cannot be applied right now


5. Performance Is Not Optional

Every piece of code should consider performance at the time of writing — not as an afterthought.

ABAP specific:

  • Prefer SELECT ... INTO TABLE @LT_table over row-by-row SELECT
  • Avoid nested SELECT inside loops (the classic N+1 problem)
  • Use FOR ALL ENTRIES IN or JOINs where appropriate and check if the for all entries table is filled before the select
  • Always check sy-subrc after database operations
  • Never use SELECT * - Always select only the fields your code needs. Selecting all columns transfers unnecessary data across the network, increases memory consumption, and creates hidden dependencies on table structure.
    ❌  Never do this SELECT * FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders.
    ✅Select only what you need SELECT vbeln, kunnr, audat FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders WHERE vkorg = @LV_sales_org.
  • Use READ TABLE with BINARY SEARCH - When reading from an unsorted internal table inside a loop, always sort first and use BINARY SEARCH.
     ✅ Sort once, read many times efficiently
SORT lt_materials BY matnr.

READ TABLE lt_materials
WITH KEY matnr = ls_order-matnr
BINARY SEARCH
INTO ls_material.


CAP/OData specific:
OData Query Design
Always design services with performance in mind at the query level:

  • Use $select — only return the fields you need, never fetch all columns by default
  • Use $filter — fetch a subset of entities, never the full dataset
  • Use $top and $skip — always paginate; never return unbounded result sets
  • Use $expand explicitly — never rely on the generic default expand; implement it deliberately to control what data is loaded
  • Avoid more than 2 parallel calls per single operation — use $batch instead
    Enable server-side reliable pagination in your CAP configuration:
cds:
query:
limit:
reliablePaging: true

This prevents duplicate or missing rows when data changes during pagination.

Data Loading

  • Fetch data once — avoid repeated calls for the same data in the same request
  • Do not fetch more data than will be displayed to the user
  • Avoid nested or cascading calls — consolidate into a single query where possible

UI5/Frontend specific

  • Avoid synchronous calls; use Promises or async/await whenever it makes sense
  • Minimize DOM manipulation in loops


Profiling Tools
When investigating performance issues:

  • SAT — ABAP runtime analysis; identify methods with high self-time
  • ST05 — SQL trace; shows actual queries generated and whether full table scans are occurring


Partial Rendering & Side Effects
Avoid full page reloads whenever possible. Use OData Side Effects (CAP/RAP) to refresh only the data that changed. Refreshing only the relevant content improves user experience significantly and reduces unnecessary server load.

 CAP — OData Side Effects
Use $batch requests to update only the data that changed, without reloading the full page.

Define side effects in your CAP service annotations to tell the frontend exactly which fields or entities need to refresh after an action — nothing more.

RAP — Partial Refresh via Actions

Design actions and determinations to return only the affected data. Avoid triggering full entity reloads when only one field changed.

Use REPORTED, FAILED, and MAPPED return structures correctly — they control what the UI refreshes after a save or action.

6. Flag Deviations - No Silent Compromises

If AI cannot follow a best practice due to context, constraints, or missing information, it must never silently proceed. It must surface the issue.

Format for flagging:

⚠️DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE

Reason: [explain why]

Recommended approach: [what should be done]

Current approach: [what was done and why]

7. Error Handling is not Optional

Every piece of code that can fail must handle failure explicitly. The happy path is not enough.

Rules:

  • Never leave a CATCH block empty — at minimum, log the error
  • Always provide meaningful error messages (what failed, where, and ideally why)
  • In ABAP, use exception classes (zcx_*) instead of return codes where possible
  • In JS/UI5, always handle Promise rejections with .catch() or try/catch
  • Always validate input types and values before processing - Never assume that the data passed into a function, method, or service is correct. Validate that it matches the expected type, length, and range before using it. Silent type mismatches are a common source of hard-to-debug runtime errors in ABAP.
    ✅Validate input before processing
IF iv_order_id IS INITIAL.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Order ID cannot be empty'.
ENDIF.
IF iv_quantity <= 0.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Quantity must be greater than zero'.
ENDIF.
  • Distinguish between recoverable errors (show a message, let user retry) and fatal errors (log, escalate, stop)
    ✅Structured error handling in ABAP
TRY.
lo_order_processor->process( iv_order_id = lv_order_id ).
CATCH zcx_order_not_found INTO lx_error.
" Order not found — inform the user and stop
MESSAGE lx_error->get_text( ) TYPE 'E'.
CATCH zcx_general_error INTO lx_error.
" Unexpected error — log and escalate
zcl_logger=>log_error( lx_error ).
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_general_error.
ENDTRY.

✅Always handle async errors in UI5

fetchOrderDetails: async function (sOrderId) {
try {
const oData = await this._callOrderService(sOrderId);
this._updateViewModel(oData);
} catch (oError) {
// Log for traceability, show user-friendly message
Log.error("fetchOrderDetails failed", oError.message, "OrderController");
MessageBox.error(this.getText("errorLoadingOrder"));
}
}

 

8. Single Responsibility

One method does one thing. One class has one purpose.

  • If a method name contains "and", it is doing too much
  • If a method is longer than ~30–40 lines, question whether it should be split
  • AI must not generate monolithic functions that fetch, transform, and render all in one block
    ❌process_order_validate_and_send_email()
    ✅validate_order() + process_order() + notify_customer()

9. Testability

Code must be written in a way that allows it to be tested in isolation.

Rules:

  • Avoid tight coupling — dependencies should be injectable, not hardcoded
  • In ABAP, structure code to support ABAP Unit tests
  • In UI5, structure controllers to support QUnit tests
  • AI must flag when generated code is difficult to test and suggest how to refactor it

10 . Version & Dependency Awareness

  • Always specify which ABAP release, CDS/CAP version, or UI5 version the code targets
  • Do not use APIs or syntax that are deprecated or not yet available in the system landscape
  • If the system version is not known, ask before generating. Do not assume.

11. Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears more than once, it belongs in a shared method, class, or utility.
AI must not copy-paste logic with minor variations — it must abstract it

12. Leave the Code Better Than You Found It

Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

  • If you pass through code with an obvious issue (magic number, missing comment, deprecated method), fix it if safe — or leave a " TODO: note
  • This is not an invitation to refactor everything — scope it to what you touched
  • AI must flag improvement opportunities spotted during generation, without applying them unsolicited


13. Avoid over-engineering

Build what is needed now, but do not close doors for tomorrow. Avoid unnecessary complexity, but design with extensibility in mind. Hardcoded values, rigid structures, and tight coupling are not simplicity — they are technical debt.

  • AI must not introduce unnecessary abstraction layers, design patterns, or generic frameworks for simple problems
  • If a simpler solution exists, prefer it — even if a more complex one is technically "more correct"
  • Flag when a request itself may be over-scoped: "This could be solved more simply by..."

14. Say When You Are Not Sure

Honesty is a feature. If AI is uncertain about the correct approach, it must say so explicitly.
When uncertain, AI must:

  • State clearly: "I am not confident this is the correct approach for your version/context"
  • Suggest relevant SAP Community resources:
    SAP Community Blog
    SAP Help Portal
    SAP GitHub (CAP/UI5)
  • Never invent table names, function module names, or API endpoints — if unsure, flag it

15. Ask for more context if needed

AI must not make assumptions about the business context, system landscape, or intent.
When to ask before generating:

  • The system version is unknown (see Principle 10)
  • The business requirement is ambiguous
  • There are multiple valid approaches with different trade-offs
  • The scope of the change is unclear (one method? one class? one package?)
  • A few seconds asking the right question saves hours of rework.

16. Go Through the Front Door

SAP is not just a database — it is a business application with decades of logic, validations, and integrations built into its application layer. Writing directly to standard tables bypasses all of that. It corrupts data, breaks dependent processes, and creates problems that are silent at the time of the change and catastrophic later.

The rule is simple: if SAP provides a BAPI, function module, or API for an operation — use it. Always.

  • Never update, insert, or delete SAP standard tables directly. Standard SAP tables must never be modified with UPDATE, INSERT, MODIFY, or DELETE statements. Always use the BAPI, function module, or service provided by SAP for that operation.

" ❌ Never do this — bypasses all SAP business logic

UPDATE vbak SET gbstk = 'C' WHERE vbeln = lv_order_id.

" ✅ Use the correct BAPI

CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING
salesdocument = lv_order_id


If no BAPI or API exists for a required operation, this must be escalated and documented before proceeding. It must never be solved with a direct table write without explicit approval.

  • Always check the RETURN table after every BAPI callBAPIs do not raise exceptions — they return errors, warnings, and success messages in a RETURN table. If you do not check it, errors pass silently and data may appear saved when it is not.
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING salesdocument = lv_order_id
TABLES return = lt_return.​

✅Always check for errors in the return table

READ TABLE lt_return
WITH KEY type = 'E'
TRANSPORTING NO FIELDS.

IF sy-subrc = 0.
" Error found — do not commit, handle it
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_bapi_error.
ENDIF.
  • Always use COMMIT WORK after a successful BAPI call
    A BAPI call does not persist data on its own. You must explicitly commit the work unit. Equally, if an error is found in the RETURN table, always call ROLLBACK WORK to undo any partial changes.
    "✅ Commit only after confirming no errors
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
EXPORTING wait = abap_true.​

" ✅ Rollback on error
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
Never use COMMIT WORK directly in BAPI-based flows — always use BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT = ABAP_TRUE to ensure the update task completes before proceeding.


⚠️This rule applies to classic ABAP and BAPI-based flows only. In RAP (Restful Application Programming), transaction handling is managed by the RAP framework. Never call COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT inside a RAP behaviour handler — the framework commits automatically after the save sequence completes successfully.


17. Deployment & Transport
This here changes from company to company. Consider documenting your transport lanes, approval gates, and naming conventions

18. Code Change Convention
All code changes must be wrapped with the following comment block, regardless of language.

*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Start
*** [Previous code or "N/A - New implementation"]
[New code here]
*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Finish


19. Inline Code Comments
When to Comment explain why, not what. The code should explain what it does. Comments explain decisions.

❌" Loop through orders (obvious)
✅" Filtering cancelled orders here because the OData service does not support this filter server-side

Your turn!

Do you use AI instructions with your team? What would you add to this list? What would you change or throw out? 

Update
Well... Something happened with the instructions AI had one set of instructions and broke it fearlessly — then apologised!

entry.title: Fixing the Orphaned Workflow Issue in SF Time Off Cancellation: withdrawWfRequest using Odata API
entry.content:
The Problem

If you're building a third-party integration either a mobile app, custom portal, or any external system that allows employees to request and cancel time off via SuccessFactors OData APIs, you may have run into this exact issue:

Employee cancels their time off request through your custom app. The EmployeeTime record correctly shows "approvalStatus = CANCELLED" in SF. But the manager still sees the request sitting in their approval inbox now showing a confusing "Cancelled" status that they can't do anything about, because the workflow instance itself was never terminated.

This is a common integration gap, and it happens because the business object and the workflow instance are two separate things in SF, and cancelling one does not automatically close the other.

This post demonstrates the full fix end-to-end, with real request/response payloads.

 

Why This Happens

Object What it represents
What updating it does
EmployeeTime recordThe actual time off data (dates, type, status)Changes the record's own status field only
WfRequest (workflow instance)The routing object sitting in the approver's inboxControls what the manager sees in their To-Do list

The EmployeeTime record and the WfRequest workflow instance are two separate objects in SF. Patching the record's approvalStatus field only changes the record itself it does not notify the workflow engine that the related approval item should close.

As a result, the workflow stays visible on the manager's screen even after the record shows CANCELLED, unless withdrawWfRequest is called explicitly to terminate that workflow instance.

 

The Full Flow: Demonstration

Step 1 - Employee cancels time off (existing working step) from Custom App

Below is the leave request detail Payload which be passed to CPI as request from custom application with Externalcode, User Id (LeaveRequestID), Time Type, Start Date and End Date

{
    "LeaveRequestID": "307eb8b817fd4e6c87f3d6ecdfc88cdf", --> External code of the leave
    "timeType": "1000",
    "userId": "test1",
    "startDate": "2026-10-01T00:00:00.000",
    "endDate": "2026-10-01T00:00:00.000"
}

Post Call: 

At this point, the time record is updated but the workflow is still active on the manager's screen. This is the gap.

Step 2 - Retrieve the associated wfRequestId

Before you can withdraw anything, you need the workflow ID tied to this specific time record. Query it via the navigation property or a filtered lookup:

GET call:

https://<api-server>/odata/v2/EmployeeTime?$select=externalCode,approvalStatus,endDate,startDate,timeType,userId,workflowRequestId&$filter=externalCode eq '${property.externalCode}' --> External code we got from mobile app ( in this case '307eb8b817fd4e6c87f3d6ecdfc88cdf')

Note: The exact navigation property name can differ depending on whether this is a standard object (EmployeeTime) or a custom MDF object . MDF objects typically expose this through a generic workflow association field configured in the object definition. Check your object's metadata ($metadata) if the property name above doesn't match your instance.

Step 3 - Withdraw the workflow (the actual fix)

Use the HTTP Adapter in CPI below screenshot to withdraw the workflow,

 

 

 

 

 


POST Call :
(use the worflow id from step 2) - https://<api-server>/odata/v2/withdrawWfRequest?wfRequestId=1937715L

API Response -

<d:WfRequestActionResponse>
 <d:element m:type="SFOData.WfRequestActionResponse">
<d:status>success</d:status>
<d:wfRequestId m:type="Edm.Int64">1937715L</d:wfRequestId>
 </d:element>
</d:WfRequestActionResponse>

The workflow instance is now terminated. It disappears from the manager's pending approvals, and the workflow history correctly reflects it as Withdrawn rather than leaving a dangling "Cancelled" item with no further action possible.

Pattern

Cancel object → Get wfRequestId → withdrawWfRequest (HTTP Adapter in CPI)

Applies to any standard or custom MDF object with workflow routing.


Error Handling:

 
Error CodeLikely Cause
COE_GENERAL_BAD_REQUESTEither the API user lacks withdrawWfRequest permission in WorkflowAllowedActionList, or the wfRequestId is invalid/already closed
404 on the wfRequestId lookupThe object may not have an active workflow (e.g., auto-approved request with no routing) — handle this gracefully and skip step 3
Permission error on withdrawConfirm this is a separate authorization from the one governing object creation/cancellation — easy to miss since the first two calls can work fine while this one fails

 

Summary

A clean cancellation flow for any workflow-routed object in SuccessFactors requires two actions, not one:

  1. Update the business object's status
  2. Explicitly withdraw the associated workflow instance via withdrawWfRequest

Skipping step 2 is what causes orphaned "Cancelled" items to linger on manager approval screens , a frustrating but entirely avoidable integration bug once you know the workflow engine and the business object are decoupled.

Hope you found this blog helpful, please leave your feedback or any suggestion in the comment. 

Thanks,
Amit
