entry.title: An End-to-End Travel Approval App with SAP CAP, HANA Cloud, and SAP Build Process Automation
entry.content:
Goal

The goal is to build a working Travel Approval application, not just a collection of disconnected demos. A user creates a travel request in a Fiori Elements application. The CAP service stores the request in SAP HANA Cloud and automatically starts an SAP Build Process Automation workflow.

The approver reviews the task in My Inbox and selects Approve or Reject, updating the corresponding Travel record in HANA Cloud.

Create Travel in Fiori
       ↓
CAP saves the active record in HANA Cloud
       ↓
CAP starts the BPA workflow automatically
       ↓
Approval task appears in SAP Build Lobby->My Inbox
       ↓
Approve → overall_status = A
Reject → overall_status = R
       ↓
Validate in Fiori, SAP Build->Monitoring, and HANA Database Explorer

Prerequisites

BTP Service / instance required
SAP Business Application Studio
SAP HANA Cloud
SAP Build Process Automation

The End-to-End Flow

  1. Create Travel entity in CDS.
  2. Expose the entity as a draft-enabled OData V4 service.
  3. Generate the Fiori Elements application.
  4. Bind the CAP project to the HANA HDI container.
  5. Build the MTA archive and deploy it to Cloud Foundry.
  6. Download the CAP metadata as an EDMX specification.
  7. Create SAP Build Actions from the EDMX and test the OData operations.
  8. Create the Travel Context, API trigger, Approval Form, and approval branches in BPA.
  9. Create a BPA service key and an API key with trigger execution permission.
  10. Add the CAP SAVE handler that starts the workflow automatically.
  11. Test from Fiori, process the task in My Inbox, monitor the instance in Build Lobby, and validate the final status in HANA.

1. Model the CDS Entity for the CAP OData V4 Service

The CDS entity is the source of truth for the Travel data. The technical UUID and the business Travel ID form the key used by the draft-enabled service and by the generated SAP Build Actions.

1.1.    Expose the Travel entity as a service

Create file srv/service.cds.

Why draft support matters: Fiori Elements creates and edits a draft first. The active Travel record is produced when the user activates or saves the draft. The CAP SAVE event is therefore the reliable point for starting the workflow.

2. Create the Fiori Elements App

Generate a List Report/Object Page application for CAPWFService.Travel. The list lets users create requests and review the current status. The Object Page captures the full Travel details.

 

Figure 1. Fiori List Report with Travel IDs in ascending order.

3. Connect to Cloud Foundry

3.1.    Cloud Foundry provides the runtime for the deployed CAP service. Log in from the BAS terminal and select the correct organization and dev space.

cf login
cf target

3.2.    Before testing SAP Build Actions, always confirm that the deployed CAP application is running:

cf start CAPWF-srv
cf app CAPWF-srv

3.3.    Expected status:

requested state: started
instances: 1/1
state: running

Important: When CAPWF-srv was stopped, every SAP Build Action returned 404 Requested route does not exist. Starting the application restored the Actions immediately.

4. Bind to a HANA Cloud HDI Container

An HDI container is an application-scoped database container. It gives the CAP application its own isolated schema inside the HANA Cloud database.

cds bind --to CAPWF-db
cds env get requires.db --profile hybrid

The hybrid profile must show the CAPWF-db instance. Start the local service against HANA:

pkill -f cds
cds watch --profile hybrid

Look for connect to db > hana and the expected HANA schema in the terminal output.

Lesson learned: The lowercase capwf-db and uppercase CAPWF-db were two separate service instances. Local Fiori and deployed BPA initially showed different record counts because they were connected to different HDI containers.

5. Generate the MTAR File

The Multi-Target Application archive packages the service, database deployer, security resources, destinations, and HTML5 content into one deployable unit.

mbt build

The archive is generated under: mta_archives/CAPWF_1.0.0.mtar

6. Deploy to HANA Cloud and Cloud Foundry

cf deploy mta_archives/CAPWF_1.0.0.mtar

The deployment runs the database deployer, binds CAPWF-srv to CAPWF-db and CAPWF-auth, and starts the application route.

cf app CAPWF-srv
cf routes
cf logs CAPWF-srv --recent

Free-tier note: Stopping applications frees runtime memory, but it also makes the CAP route unavailable. Start CAPWF-srv again before testing browser URLs or SAP Build Actions.

7. Connect to the HANA DB Explorer and Add the HDI Container

7.1.    Open SAP HANA Database Explorer.

7.2.    Choose Add Database or Add HDI Container.

7.3.    Select the CAPWF-db HDI container.

7.4.    Expand Catalog and Tables.

7.5.    Open the Travel table data and compare the record count with the Fiori app.

7.6.    After approval or rejection, refresh the table and verify overall_status.

Figure 2. CAPWF-db added to SAP HANA Database Explorer.

8. Download the Metadata File as EDMX

The metadata document describes the OData V4 service, entity fields, keys, draft properties, and custom actions. SAP Build uses this specification to generate reusable Actions.

/service/CAPWFService/$metadata

Open the metadata->right-click->Save as .edmx file

Open the local BAS port 4004 metadata URL, save the XML as CAPWFService.edmx, and verify that it contains:

  • EntitySet Name="Travel"
  • The Travel entity fields and keys
  • Draft operations
  • Action Name="submitForApproval" IsBound="true"

9. Create SAP Build Actions

9.1. Open SAP Build Lobby -> Actions -> Create.

9.2. Choose Upload API Specification.

9.3. Upload CAPWFService.edmx.

9.4. Create the Action project CAPWFService3.

9.5. Select the required Travel operations. The POC selected all 13 generated operations.

10.   Open Settings and configure the destination and URL prefix.

SettingValue
DestinationCAPWF-srv
URL Prefix/service/CAPWFService
CSRFDisabled for this POC
Destination authenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials

11.   Test the Actions before publishing

11.1.   Get entities from Travel should return 200 OK and all records. - see the image below

11.2.   Get entity from Travel by key should return the selected record using ID, travel_id, and  IsActiveEntity=true.

11.3.   Update entity in Travel should be validated independently before adding it to the process.

11.4.   Release and Publish only after direct tests succeed.

cf logs CAPWF-srv cf app CAPWF-srv cf start CAPWF-srv -->You can see the Instances are up and Running 1/14.       The root cause may simply be a stopped application.

Troubleshooting shortcut: If all Actions suddenly return 404 and no request reaches, run the below commands in new Terminal.

 

Figure 2. CAPWFService3 Action test returning 200 OK.

12. Steps in SAP Build Process Automation

12.1.Create the project and artifacts

12.2.Create the project RAP110_Travel_Workflow.

12.3.Create the process of Travel Approval Processing.

12.4.Create the Travel Context datatype.

12.5.Create a Travel Approval Trigger as an API trigger.

12.6.Create the Approval Form and map the Travel fields.

12.7.Add Approve and Reject outcomes.

12.8.Add Update entity in Travel from the published CAPWFService3 dependency.

12.9.Map the keys and set overall_status to A in Approve and R in Reject.

13. Travel Context fields

FieldData Type
TravelUUIDString
TravelIDNumber
IsActiveEntityBoolean
agency_idNumber
customer_idNumber
begin_dateDate
end_dateDate
booking_feeNumber
total_priceNumber
currency_codeString
descriptionString
overall_statusString

14. Approval Form recipient

When a human starts the workflow manually, Started By is the signed-in user. When CAP starts the process using client credentials, Started By is a technical client. For the POC, the Approval Form recipient was set to the intended email address, so the work item appeared in My Inbox. A production design should pass an ApproverEmail value or determine the approver through business rules.

15. Add and Delete Dependencies

15.1.A process can use only released and published Action projects through Dependencies.

15.2.Open the editable BPA project and switch to Dependencies.

15.3.Add the published CAPWFService3 Action project.

15.4.If an old Action dependency is removed, delete any orphaned process nodes that show blank Inputs.

15.5.Re-add the Actions from CAPWFService3 and remap their inputs.

15.6.To remove a dependency, select it, choose Settings, and select Delete.

15.7.If an Action project cannot be deleted, remove consuming dependencies and delete its released versions first.

16. Create an API Key in SAP Build

The CAP application starts the process as a technical client. It therefore needs both OAuth client credentials and an SAP Build API key that is authorized to execute the trigger.

16.1.Open SAP Build -> Control Tower -> API Keys, or Public Environment -> API Keys.

16.2.Choose Add API Key.

16.3.Enter a meaningful name, such as CAPWF_Auto_Start.

16.4.Select the Public environment.

16.5.Enable trigger_execute. This is the minimum scope needed to execute the API trigger.

16.6.Create the key and copy it immediately. The value is displayed only once.

17. Build Process Automation - Manual Workflow Test Using the Payload

Before automating the trigger from CAP, manually prove the deployed process and payload schema.

17.1.Open Control Tower -> Environments -> Public -> Triggers.

17.2.Open Travel Approval Trigger.

17.3.Choose Start New Instance.

17.4.Paste only the process context expected by the dialog, with travelContext as the root object.

17.5.Start the instance and confirm it appears in Monitoring.

17.6.Open My Inbox and process the task.

17.7.Confirm the instance completes and the Travel status is updated.

{
"travelContext": {
   "TravelUUID": "<UUID>",
   "TravelID": 15,
   "IsActiveEntity": true,
   "agency_id": 70015,
   "customer_id": 70015,
   "begin_date": "2026-10-02",
   "end_date": "2026-10-16",
   "booking_fee": 150,
   "total_price": 150,
   "currency_code": "INR",
   "description": "Travel request",
   "overall_status": "W"
}
}

18. List of Terminal Commands to Get BPA Keys

cf create-service-key BPA cap-bpa-key
cf service-key BPA cap-bpa-key

From the BPA service key, record these values securely: clientid, clientsecret, and URL. The token endpoint is the URL value plus /oauth/token.

Do not mix credentials: CAPWF-auth credentials protect the CAP application. BPA service-key credentials authenticate the call to SAP Build Process Automation. Using CAPWF-auth credentials caused 401 invalid_client / Bad credentials.

19. Start the Workflow Automatically from CAP

The Fiori application activates a draft when the user saves a new Travel. CAP handles that lifecycle through the SAVE event. The handler builds the exact trigger payload, obtains an OAuth token, sends the BPA API key, and creates the workflow instance.

// create a file in srv/service.js

this.after('SAVE', 'Travel', async (data, req) => {
   const travel = req.data;

   const workflowPayload = {
       definitionId:
         'us10.e66895ddtrial.rap110travelworkflow.travelApprovalProcessing',
       context: {
           travelContext: {
               TravelUUID: travel.ID,
               TravelID: travel.travel_id,
               IsActiveEntity: true,
               agency_id: travel.agency_id,
               customer_id: travel.customer_id,
               begin_date: travel.begin_date,
               end_date: travel.end_date,
               booking_fee: Number(travel.booking_fee),
               total_price: Number(travel.total_price),
               currency_code: travel.currency_code,
               description: travel.description,
               overall_status: travel.overall_status
           }
       }
   };

   // 1. Get an OAuth token with BPA client credentials.
   // 2. POST workflowPayload to BPA_WORKFLOW_URL.
   // 3. Send Authorization: Bearer <token> and api-key headers.
});

20. Verify in BAS with Three Terminals

20.1.   Terminal 1 - Run local CAP with BPA credentials

export BPA_CLIENT_ID='<BPA service-key clientid>'
export BPA_CLIENT_SECRET='<BPA service-key clientsecret>'
export BPA_TOKEN_URL='<BPA service-key url>/oauth/token'
export BPA_API_KEY='<SAP Build Public environment API key>'
export BPA_WORKFLOW_URL='https://spa-api-gateway-bpi-us-prod.cfapps.us10.hana.ondemand.com/workflow/rest/v1/workflow-instances'

pkill -f cds
cds watch --profile hybrid

20.2.   Terminal 2 - Confirm the deployed CAP app is running

cf start CAPWF-srv
cf app CAPWF-srv

20.3.   Terminal 3 - Watch deployed CAP requests

cf logs CAPWF-srv

A successful automatic start prints:

BPA workflow started for Travel 5
Workflow instance ID: <generated instance ID>

Session behavior: The export commands apply only to the current terminal session.

After BAS signs out or a new terminal is opened, export the variables again before cds watch.

21. Test Directly from the Fiori Application

21.1.Confirm Terminal 1 has BPA environment variables, and cds watch is running.

21.2.Confirm CAPWF-srv is 1/1 running if the workflow will call CAP through SAP Build Actions.

21.3.Open the Fiori Preview.

21.4.Create a new Travel record with overall_status W.

21.5.Save the record.

21.6.Watch Terminal 1 for the workflow instance ID.

21.7.Open SAP Build My Inbox and process the Travel task.

21.8.Refresh the Fiori List Report and confirm A or R.

22. My Inbox - Approve or Reject

The approver opens the Travel task, reviews the Travel fields, and chooses Approve or Reject. The process follows the corresponding branch and calls the CAP update Action. The completed workflow should disappear from My Inbox and appear as Completed in Monitoring.

If My Inbox is empty: Open the instance Logs. If the recipient is a technical client instead of the intended user, revise the Approval Form recipient mapping and deploy a new version.

23. Monitor Workflow Instances

23.1.Open SAP Build -> Monitoring -> Processes and Workflows.

23.2.Open Travel Approval Processing.

23.3.Filter by Running, Error, or Completed.

23.4.Open an instance and inspect Logs to see each executed step.

23.5.Open Context to confirm startEvent.travelContext values.

23.6.Use the instance ID printed by CAP to correlate the application request with the workflow instance.

Figure 4. Completed Travel Approval Processing instance.

24. Validate in the HDI Container

24.1.Open SAP HANA Database Explorer and refresh CAPWF-db.

24.2.Open the Travel table data.

24.3.Locate the Travel ID used in the test.

24.4.Confirm W before approval.

24.5.Confirm A after approval or R after rejection.

24.6.Compare the result with the Fiori List Report.

What Broke, Why It Broke, and the Fix

pkill -f cds​then start one runtime.

SymptomRoot causeFix
Fiori showed more records than BPA/HANADifferent HDI containers were usedBind local hybrid runtime to CAPWF-db.
Port 4004 already in useAn old cds process was still running 
Actions returned 404 route do not existCAPWF-srv was stoppedcf start CAPWF-srv and confirm 1/1 running.
Metadata returned UnauthorizedXSUAA was protecting the deployed serviceUse OAuth2ClientCredentials in CAPWF-srv destination.
BPA trigger returned invalid_clientCAPWF-auth credentials were used instead of BPA service-key credentialsUse cf service-key BPA cap-bpa-key values.
Workflow URL was Invalid URLEnvironment variables were missing after BAS re-loginExport variables in the same terminal before cds watch.
Workflow instance existed but My Inbox was emptyStarted By resolved to the technical OAuth clientUse an explicit recipient or dynamic ApproverEmail.
Action Inputs were blankProcess node referenced a removed Action dependencyDelete and re-add the node from the active dependency.
Travel ID sorting was inconsistentPresentation Variant did not reference the LineItem visualizationAdd Visualizations: ['@UI.LineItem'].
SAVE handler received data differently than CREATEFiori used draft activationUse after SAVE and req.data.

Conclusion

The solution combines Fiori Elements for data entry, CAP for service logic, HANA Cloud for persistence, and SAP Build Process Automation for approval. Success depends on aligning code, runtime state, destinations, credentials, recipients, dependencies, and HDI bindings. Once aligned, users can create, approve or reject, and view Travel requests in one application.

For similar integrations, test each connection independently: Fiori–CAP, CAP–HANA, CAP–BPA, BPA–CAP Actions, and task assignment. This turns a complex landscape into manageable checkpoints.

References

  • SAP Help: SAP Build Process Automation authorizations
  • SAP Help: SAP Business Application Studio roles
  • SAP Help: API Keys 
  • SAP Help: Execute an API Trigger
  • SAP Help: Use API Keys
  • SAP Help: Configure an API Trigger to Start a Process

entry.title: Retrieve Specific User Information from SAP SuccessFactors Using SAP Cloud Integration (OData V2)
entry.content:
Introduction

In many SAP integration scenarios, we need to retrieve information about a specific employee or user from SAP SuccessFactors instead of fetching the entire user dataset.

For example, an external application may send a user ID to SAP Cloud Integration (CPI), and the integration flow must retrieve the corresponding user's details, such as their username, first name, last name, and email address, from SAP SuccessFactors.

In this blog, we will build an integration flow in SAP Integration Suite – Cloud Integration that retrieves user-specific information from SAP SuccessFactors using the OData V2 adapter.

The flow accepts an incoming request, reads the requested user ID, queries the SuccessFactors User entity, processes the response using a Groovy Script, and returns the result to the calling application.

1. Prerequisites

Before implementing this integration flow, ensure that you have the following:

  1. SAP SuccessFactors API access: You must have access to an SAP SuccessFactors environment with API permissions.

  2. SuccessFactors credentials: You need a valid API-enabled user ID and password, along with the appropriate company ID (company code/Company ID used by your SuccessFactors tenant).

  3. SuccessFactors API endpoint: For this example, we will use the following demo endpoint:

    https://apisalesdemo8.successfactors.com

  4. SAP Integration Suite access: You must have access to Cloud Integration and permission to create, configure, and deploy integration flows.

  5. User entity permissions: The SuccessFactors API user must have the necessary permissions to read the User entity and the required fields.

  6. Testing tool: Postman or another HTTP client can be used to send a request to the deployed integration flow.

Important: The demo endpoint is used for illustration. Make sure your tenant, Company ID, credentials, and API permissions are valid before testing. Do not expose passwords or other credentials in the blog or in screenshots.

2. Integration Scenario

The objective is to retrieve information for one specific user based on a user ID supplied in the incoming request.

For example, if the incoming request contains the user ID 100045, the integration flow queries SAP SuccessFactors and returns the matching user's details.

The fields retrieved in this example are:

  • userId

  • username

  • firstName

  • lastName

  • email

Instead of retrieving all users, we use an OData $filter expression to select only the record matching the supplied user ID.

3. Integration Flow Design

Create an integration flow named:

SF_Get_UserSpecific_data

The flow consists of the following main steps:

  1. HTTPS Sender

  2. Content Modifier

  3. Request Reply

  4. SuccessFactors Receiver using the OData V2 adapter

  5. Groovy Script

  6. Message End

The overall processing sequence is:

Incoming HTTP Request → Content Modifier → Request Reply → SuccessFactors OData V2 → Groovy Script → Response

The HTTPS Sender receives the request from the external application. The Content Modifier extracts or prepares the user ID as an exchange property. The Request Reply step invokes SAP SuccessFactors through the receiver channel. After receiving the response, the Groovy Script processes the payload before it is returned to the caller.

IFLOW

 

4. Create the Integration Flow

Log in to SAP Integration Suite and navigate to Design → Integrations and APIs.

Open your integration package or create a new package. Select Add → Integration Flow, provide the name SF_Get_UserSpecific_data, and save it.

Open the integration flow in the editor.

Step 4.1: Configure the HTTPS Sender

Add an HTTPS Sender adapter to the sender participant and connect it to the integration process.

Configure the sender so that an external client can invoke the integration flow through HTTP.

The exact endpoint path and authentication settings depend on your tenant configuration. For production scenarios, configure suitable authentication and authorization.

The calling application will send the user ID in the request payload. We will use that value in the subsequent steps.

 

 

Step 4.2: Configure the Content Modifier

Add a Content Modifier after the Start event.

The purpose of this step is to extract the incoming user ID and store it in an exchange property named userID.

For this example, assume the incoming request is XML:

<UserRequest>
    <userID>10025</userID>
</UserRequest>

If the sender payload is XML, configure the Content Modifier or a preceding transformation step to extract the value using the appropriate XMLPath expression.

For example, where supported by your configuration, use the XMLPath expression:

//userID

Create the exchange property as follows:

Field Value

NameuserID
TypeExpression
Value//userID

The exact expression syntax depends on the Content Modifier field and how the incoming message is represented. If your flow receives XML or plain text instead of JSON, configure the extraction accordingly.

The important result is that the exchange property userID contains the requested user's ID before the Request Reply step is executed.

Note: The SuccessFactors query uses ${property.userID}. Therefore, make sure the property name is exactly userID, including capitalization.

Content Modifier

 

5. Configure the SuccessFactors OData V2 Receiver

Add a Request Reply step to the integration process and connect it to a receiver participant configured with the SuccessFactors adapter.

Create or configure the receiver channel using the SuccessFactors OData V2 adapter.

Step 5.1: Configure the connection

Use the following connection details as a starting point:

Configuration Value

AdapterSuccessFactors OData V2
Address/Service URLhttps://apisalesdemo8.successfactors.com
AuthenticationAs supported and configured for your SuccessFactors tenant
Company IDYour SuccessFactors Company ID
User IDYour API-enabled SuccessFactors user
PasswordThe corresponding password, if required by the selected authentication method

Store credentials securely using the supported security material and authentication configuration in your tenant. Do not hardcode passwords in scripts or expose them in screenshots.

Depending on your adapter configuration, the entity, operation, resource path, and query options may be configured in the receiver channel.

 

Step 5.2: Select the OData entity

For this scenario, use the SuccessFactors User entity.

The User entity provides basic user information, including identifiers and selected personal or contact fields, subject to the permissions granted to the API user.

Configure the operation to read/query the User entity.

Step 5.3: Configure the OData query

Use the following query options:

$select=userId,username,firstName,lastName,email&$filter=userId eq '${property.userID}'

This query contains two important OData options.

$select — Specify the fields to retrieve

$select=userId,username,firstName,lastName,email

This restricts the response to the five fields required for the scenario, rather than requesting every available property.

$filter — Retrieve the matching user

$filter=userId eq '${property.userID}'

This filters the User entity using the userID exchange property populated by the Content Modifier.

If the property contains 100045, the effective filter is:

userId eq '100045'

The resulting query requests only the selected fields for the matching user.

 

6. Add the Groovy Script

-->If you want to log a attachment for the output payload , you can use this groovy script or else just skip the step.

import com.sap.gateway.ip.core.customdev.util.Message

def Message processData(Message message) {

    // Read payload as String
    def body = message.getBody(String)

    // Get Content-Type header
    def headers = message.getHeaders()
    def contentType = headers.get("Content-Type")

    // Default to text/plain if Content-Type is not available
    if (contentType == null || contentType.trim().isEmpty()) {
        contentType = "text/plain"
    }

    // Get Message Processing Log
    def messageLog = messageLogFactory.getMessageLog(message)

    if (messageLog != null) {
        messageLog.addAttachmentAsString("Payload", body, contentType)
    }

    return message
}

 

7. Deploy the Integration Flow

After configuring the sender, Content Modifier, Request Reply, receiver channel, and Groovy Script:

  1. Save the integration flow.

  2. Validate the configuration and resolve any errors.

  3. Configure the required security material and authentication settings.

  4. Deploy the integration flow.

  5. Open the deployed artifact and verify its status.

Once deployed successfully, the HTTPS endpoint can be invoked by an authorized client.

8. Test the Integration Flow Using Postman

Open Postman and create a new HTTP request.

Step 8.1: Configure the request

Use the HTTPS endpoint generated for your deployed integration flow.

Select the HTTP method configured for the sender, typically GET when sending a request body.

Configure the appropriate authentication method for the HTTPS sender and add the content type header:

Content-Type: application/xml

Step 8.2: Send the request payload

In the Body section, select raw → XML and provide:

<UserRequest>
    <userID>10025</userID>
</UserRequest>

Replace 100045 with a valid user ID available in your SuccessFactors tenant.

 

 

Step 8.3: Verify the response

-->My Response from successfactors 

 

Conclusion

In this blog, we explored how to retrieve specific user information from SAP SuccessFactors using SAP Integration Suite – Cloud Integration and the OData V2 adapter.

By combining an HTTPS Sender, Content Modifier, Request Reply, SuccessFactors receiver, and optional Groovy Script, we can build an integration flow that dynamically retrieves user information based on an incoming user ID.

The key part of the implementation is the OData query:

$select=userId,username,firstName,lastName,email&$filter=userId eq '${property.userID}'

This approach reduces unnecessary data retrieval and provides a reusable pattern for integrations that require user-specific information from SuccessFactors.

Thank you for reading. Feel free to share your questions, suggestions, or implementation experiences in the comments.

entry.title: Implementing Mass Approval for SRM Documents via OData Batch/Changeset Processing
entry.content:
1. Why a Custom Function Import, Not a Loop of Individual Calls

The most obvious approach — have the Fiori app call the single-item approval Function Import once per selected document, in a loop on the frontend — technically works, but it's a poor fit for this use case:

  • Each call is its own HTTP round trip, which is slow for a batch of any real size.
  • There's no natural "all or nothing" semantics — a network hiccup partway through a client-side loop leaves you with an inconsistent partial state and no clean way to know exactly where it stopped.
  • You lose the ability to give the user one consolidated result screen; you'd have to stitch that together client-side from N separate responses.

Routing it through OData's native $batch changeset mechanism instead means the whole batch is one HTTP request, SAP Gateway hands you the individual operations to process, and you control the commit/rollback boundary explicitly — which turned out to matter a lot once I hit the rollback requirement below.

2. Declaring the Function Import and Routing to It

The Fiori app calls a single custom Function Import (docWorkflowMassApproval in my case) once, passing all selected work item IDs and the chosen action as part of a changeset. In CHANGESET_PROCESS, I route based on which function import fired — this pattern is worth keeping even if you only have one mass-action function import today, because it's the natural extension point if you add a second one later (mass forward, mass delegate, etc.) without restructuring anything:

METHOD /iwbep/if_mgw_appl_srv_runtime~changeset_process.

  DATA: ls_request  TYPE /iwbep/if_mgw_appl_types=>ty_s_changeset_request,
        lo_func_req TYPE REF TO /iwbep/if_mgw_req_func_import.

  READ TABLE it_changeset_request INTO ls_request INDEX 1.
  IF sy-subrc = 0.
    TRY.
        lo_func_req ?= ls_request-request_context.
        DATA(lv_function_import) = lo_func_req->get_function_import_name( ).

        CASE lv_function_import.
          WHEN 'docWorkflowMassApproval'.
            CALL METHOD me->wf_mass_appr_changeset_process
              EXPORTING
                it_changeset_request  = it_changeset_request
              CHANGING
                ct_changeset_response = ct_changeset_response.
          WHEN OTHERS.
            " reserved for future mass-action function imports
        ENDCASE.

      CATCH /iwbep/cx_mgw_busi_exception INTO DATA(lo_busi_exc).
        mo_context->get_message_container( )->add_message_from_exception(
          io_exception = lo_busi_exc ).
      CATCH /iwbep/cx_mgw_tech_exception INTO DATA(lo_tech_exc).
        mo_context->get_message_container( )->add_message_from_exception(
          io_exception = lo_tech_exc ).
    ENDTRY.
  ENDIF.

  me->log_messages( ).
ENDMETHOD.

I'll be honest — I initially wrote this with a plain LOOP AT it_changeset_request, and only later realized that for a single function-import-driven batch (as opposed to a mix of entity create/update operations), reading just the first entry to determine the function import name and delegating the whole table onward to the dedicated handler method was cleaner than looping twice. Small thing, but it made the method easier to reason about.

3. Processing Each Work Item — And Why the Per-Item Check Matters

Inside the dedicated handler, each selected work item gets resolved from its workflow ID down to the underlying SRM document GUID, validated, and then decided on individually — even though they all arrived in one batch:

METHOD wf_mass_appr_changeset_process.

  DATA: ls_request  TYPE /iwbep/if_mgw_appl_types=>ty_s_changeset_request,
        ls_response TYPE /iwbep/if_mgw_appl_types=>ty_s_changeset_response,
        lo_func_req TYPE REF TO /iwbep/if_mgw_req_func_import,
        ls_mass_approval TYPE ysc_st_wf_mass_approval,
        lt_params   TYPE /iwbep/t_mgw_name_value_pair,
        lv_decision TYPE char20.

  LOOP AT it_changeset_request INTO ls_request.
    CLEAR: ls_response, ls_mass_approval, lv_decision.

    lo_func_req ?= ls_request-request_context.
    lt_params = lo_func_req->get_parameters( ).

    ls_mass_approval = VALUE #(
      wiid   = VALUE #( lt_params[ name = 'WIID' ]-value OPTIONAL )
      action = VALUE #( lt_params[ name = 'ACTION' ]-value OPTIONAL ) ).

    CASE ls_mass_approval-action.
      WHEN 'APPROVE'. lv_decision = 'APPROVED'.
      WHEN 'REJECT'.  lv_decision = 'REJECTED'.
      WHEN OTHERS.    CONTINUE.
    ENDCASE.

    " Resolve work item -> object instance -> SRM document GUID
    SELECT SINGLE top_wi_id FROM swwwihead
      INTO @DATA(lv_top_wi_id) WHERE wi_id = @LS_mass_approval-wiid.

    IF lv_top_wi_id IS NOT INITIAL.
      SELECT SINGLE instid FROM sww_wi2obj
        INTO @DATA(lv_instid)
        WHERE top_wi_id = @LV_top_wi_id AND wi_id = @LS_mass_approval-wiid.

      IF lv_instid IS NOT INITIAL.
        SELECT SINGLE object_id, guid FROM crmd_orderadm_h
          INTO @DATA(ls_header) WHERE guid = @LV_instid.

        IF ls_header-guid IS NOT INITIAL.
          " Validate the document is actually in a decidable state before touching workflow
          CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PROCDOC_CHECK'
            EXPORTING
              i_guid             = ls_header-guid
              iv_check_all       = 'X'
              iv_check_all_items = 'X'
            TABLES
              e_messages         = DATA(lt_check_messages).

          CALL FUNCTION '/SAPSRM/FU_WF_RFC_DECISION'
            EXPORTING
              iv_header_guid = ls_header-guid
              iv_mode        = 'APPROVAL'
              iv_wiid        = ls_mass_approval-wiid
              iv_decision    = lv_decision
              iv_approver    = sy-uname
            TABLES
              message_lines  = DATA(lt_messages)
            EXCEPTIONS
              OTHERS         = 1.

          " ... build per-item success/error message into gt_messages here ...
        ENDIF.
      ENDIF.
    ENDIF.

    copy_data_to_ref( EXPORTING is_data = ls_mass_approval
                       CHANGING  cr_data = ls_response-entity_data ).
    ls_response-operation_no = ls_request-operation_no.
    ls_response-headers      = ls_request-request_headers.
    APPEND ls_response TO ct_changeset_response.
  ENDLOOP.
ENDMETHOD.

The BBP_PROCDOC_CHECK call before the decision matters more than it might look — without it, you can end up attempting a workflow decision on a document that's technically still inconsistent (an item was changed by someone else in the same window, for instance), and the resulting error is a lot less clear to the end user than catching it explicitly beforehand and surfacing a proper message.

4. The Rollback Decision — Where I Went Back and Forth

This is the part I spent the most time actually thinking about, not coding. CHANGESET_END is where you decide whether to commit or roll back the whole batch:

METHOD /iwbep/if_mgw_appl_srv_runtime~changeset_end.
  IF line_exists( gt_messages[ type = 'E' ] ).
    ROLLBACK WORK.
  ENDIF.
  CLEAR gt_messages.
ENDMETHOD.

My first instinct was: if any item in the batch fails, roll back everything — clean, predictable, "all or nothing." But that's actually the wrong behavior for this specific use case. If an approver selects twenty documents and one of them fails validation (say, it was already decided by someone else in the meantime), rolling back the other nineteen successful decisions along with it is a genuinely bad user experience — the approver did real work processing nineteen documents correctly, and an unrelated failure on the twentieth would silently undo all of it.

I ended up not using a blanket rollback-on-any-error approach in the final version — instead tracking per-item success/failure in the message container and committing whatever succeeded, while clearly reporting which specific items failed and why. The all-or-nothing rollback pattern shown above is the simpler default and is genuinely the right call for scenarios where partial success is meaningless (e.g., a multi-step document creation where a half-created record is worse than no record) — but for a mass-decision scenario where each item is independent, per-item error reporting with partial commit is usually what the business actually wants. Worth deciding this deliberately rather than defaulting to whichever pattern you copy from an example.

5. Deferred Mode — Why CHANGESET_BEGIN Still Matters Here

Even with a single function import driving everything, CHANGESET_BEGIN is where you tell the framework whether operations need to be deferred and processed together rather than individually:

METHOD /iwbep/if_mgw_appl_srv_runtime~changeset_begin.
  TRY.
      LOOP AT it_operation_info INTO DATA(ls_operation_info).
        IF ls_operation_info-operation_type = 'CE'
        OR ls_operation_info-operation_type = 'UE'
        OR ls_operation_info-operation_type = 'EA'.
          cv_defer_mode = abap_true.
          EXIT.
        ENDIF.
      ENDLOOP.
    CATCH /iwbep/cx_mgw_busi_exception.
    CATCH /iwbep/cx_mgw_tech_exception.
      RETURN.
  ENDTRY.
ENDMETHOD.

'EA' (Execute Action / function import execution) is the operation type that matters for this scenario — setting cv_defer_mode = abap_true when it's present is what makes the framework hand you the whole changeset together in CHANGESET_PROCESS instead of processing entries independently, which is a prerequisite for the batch-level rollback decision in the previous section to even be meaningful.

entry.title: OData POST Returning 403 "CSRF Token Validation Failed"
entry.content:
While testing a custom approve/reject OData service from Postman, my GET requests worked on the first try and my POST didn't. The response was the familiar one:

403 Forbidden
CSRF token validation failed

1. The Shortcut: ~CHECK_CSRF_TOKEN = 0 in SICF (Test Systems Only)

Sometimes you just need to see whether your ABAP logic works and the token handshake is getting in the way. In that situation you can switch the check off for the service node:

  1. Run transaction SICF.
  2. Navigate to default_host → sap → opu → odata → sap (or your own namespace node, if the service lives in a customer namespace).
  3. Find the node of your custom OData service and double-click it.
  4. Click GUI Configuration.
  5. In the parameter list, add the parameter ~CHECK_CSRF_TOKEN with the value 0.
  6. Save, then test the POST again.

2. The Proper Fix: Fetch the Token (and Keep the Cookies)

Request 1 (token fetch):

 
GET https://<host>:<port>/sap/opu/odata/sap/<YOUR_SERVICE>/
Headers:
  Authorization    : <your auth>
  x-csrf-token     : Fetch
  sap-language     : EN

Look at the response headers: you should see x-csrf-token: <long token string>.

Request 2 (the actual POST):

 
POST https://<host>:<port>/sap/opu/odata/sap/<YOUR_SERVICE>/<YourEntitySet>
Headers:
  Authorization    : <your auth>
  x-csrf-token     : <token from request 1>
  Content-Type     : application/json
  Accept           : application/json
  X-Requested-With : XMLHttpRequest
  sap-language     : EN

Two practical points:

  • Cookies matter as much as the token. The token is tied to the server-side session. Postman keeps a cookie jar and sends the session cookie automatically, which is why "it works in Postman" and then fails in a script or another tool that sends the token but drops the cookie.
  • Tokens aren't forever. If the session times out or you change user/client between the two calls, the token stops being valid. Just fetch a fresh one.

3. The Headers That Cause "Mystery" Errors

Even with a valid token, a POST can still fail because of a missing or wrong header. This is the checklist I'd run through:

Header Value Why it matters

AuthorizationBasic / Bearer as per your systemWithout valid auth you get 401 or a login page instead of data
x-csrf-tokenFetch on the GET, the returned token on the POSTThe core of the 403
Content-Typeapplication/json (for $batch: multipart/mixed; boundary=...)Missing or wrong value typically gives 415 Unsupported Media Type
Acceptapplication/jsonWithout it, many services answer in XML (Atom), which can look like "wrong response format"
X-Requested-WithXMLHttpRequestMarks the call as an AJAX-style request. In my experience it helps get a clean 401/403 instead of an HTML login/redirect page when authentication fails
sap-languageEN (or your language)Controls the language of messages returned by your service
sap-clientClient number, if the system needs itCalls can land in the wrong client otherwise, and the token from one client is not valid in another

Headers like Content-Length, Host, Postman-Token, User-Agent, Accept-Encoding and Connection are added by Postman itself ("calculated when request is sent"), so you don't need to maintain them manually.

entry.title: From SOAP to RAP: Choosing a Web Service Technology in S/4HANA
entry.content:
1. Introduction

Over the years, SAP has introduced several generations of web service technology, and anyone starting a new integration project on S/4HANA today can easily lose track of which option actually fits the use case. Should an existing BAPI be released as a SOAP service? Should a classic OData v2 service be built with the Gateway Service Builder? Or is it better to go straight to RAP and OData v4, and if so, which flavor of RAP? This article is a practical, comparison-oriented overview for architects and developers who need to make that call. It is not a deep dive into any of the single technologies.

Scope. To keep the comparison practical, this article is limited to HTTP-based technologies that run entirely inside the S/4HANA system. In other words, it covers options that work without provisioning separate components such as SAP BTP Integration Suite or Event Mesh.

Read vs. write. All example calls are deliberately read-only. This keeps the examples short and comparable across technologies, without the extra complexity of create/update/delete semantics. Every technology section nevertheless explains how write access differs, so the full picture is covered.

Running example. To make the comparison concrete, every section uses the same fictional scenario: retrieving a business partner’s name and address. The data comes from the tables BUT000 (general business partner data), ADRC (address data) and BUT020 (mapping between the two). This is a small join, but a realistic and common one in S/4HANA projects, and complex enough to show how each technology copes with more than a flat, single-table lookup.

A decision matrix at the end of the article compares the technologies across several criteria: future viability, how much of the interface is defined by the developer versus dictated by the respective framework, the degree of manual implementation effort and the technical basis involved.

 

2. SOAP (RFC/BAPI released as a web service)

How it works: This is the most traditional way of exposing web service in S/4 HANA. An existing RFC-enabled function module or BAPI is released via the SOA-Manager, which generates a WSDL from the function module’s signature (import/export parameters, tables etc.). The function module itself is the implementation, so no additional code has to be written.

Implementation: First, an RFC-enabled function module is selected for exposure, either a standard one or a self-written one. A wizard in the Function Builder then creates the service definition. Alternatively, the service definition can be created in the Object Navigator (SE80). In both cases, the service is subsequently configured and activated as a runtime service in the SOA-Manager.

For the running example, this could mean either developing a custom function module that performs the table join, or choosing a standard one such as the BAPI BAPI_BUPA_ADDRESS_GETDETAIL.

Example call: Unlike the REST-style URLs discussed below, the endpoint of a SOAP service can contain multiple operations. The operation to be called is specified inside the XML body. A fictional endpoint might look like this:

POST https://<system>.example.com:44300/sap/bc/srt/rfc/sap/z_bp_address_read/300/z_bp_address_read/z_bp_address_read

Content-Type: text/xml; charset=utf-8

The HTTP request body wraps the operation and its import parameters in a <soap:Envelope>/<soap:Body> structure. The response mirrors the export parameters and tables back as XML.

Write access: For create/update, a write-enabled function module is released in the same way as a read-only one, for example the BAPIs BAPI_BUPA_CREATE and BAPI_BUPA_ADDRESS_ADD. Transaction handling is usually done server-side inside the function module, although client-steered commit handling is possible as well.

Error handling: Errors can surface on three different levels: Technical failures are reported via the HTTP status code (e.g. 500). SOAP Faults are standardized error structures inside the SOAP envelope, containing a fault code and message, and are usually returned together with HTTP status 500, for example for invalid request XML or an uncaught exception in the function module. Business errors such as “business partner not found” often arrive as a valid response with a RETURN table (e.g. BAPIRET2) and a message type like E, but can also be raised as SOAP Faults. Consumers therefore need to evaluate the HTTP status, the SOAP Fault and the business-level return structure.

Other features: The service’s capabilities are described in a metadata file following the Web Service Description Language (WSDL). Further features, such as switching between XML and JSON, filtering, or paging for high-volume calls, are either not feasible or have to be implemented manually in each function module.

When to use it: SOAP-released BAPIs can mainly be understood as legacy. SAP does not recommend this approach for new development, and hasn’t for some time. It can still be a reasonable choice when a function module already does exactly what is required and no suitable CDS views or standard OData services exist. In most other cases, the strategically recommended path is found in the later sections of this article, particularly RAP with OData v4.

 

3. OData v2 (SAP Gateway / SEGW)

How it works: The SAP Gateway Service Builder introduced a structured way of exposing data as a REST-based service following the OData v2 protocol. Entities and their relationships are modelled in transaction SEGW, while the actual data retrieval is implemented manually in generated ABAP classes, typically by redefining methods such as GET_ENTITYSET or GET_ENTITY. The resulting service follows OData v2 conventions for addressing, filtering and other query options.

Implementation: The typical path starts with creating a project in the Service Builder (SEGW), where the entity types and entity sets are defined. In the running example these would be BusinessPartner and BusinessPartnerAddress, including their relationship. After generating the development artifacts, the data provider class is implemented, for example by calling a suitable read BAPI or by selecting directly from the underlying tables or views inside GET_ENTITYSET. Finally, the service is activated and registered in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE, which makes it callable.

Example call: OData’s URL conventions make reading a specific business partner and its address look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/opu/odata/sap/ZBP_ADDRESS_V2/BusinessPartnerAddressSet('P1001')?$expand=_toAddress

Accept: application/json

Since this is a GET call, no HTTP body is required for read access.

Error handling: Errors come back as standard HTTP status codes (404 for a business partner that doesn’t exist, 400 for a malformed filter, and so on), together with an OData-standard JSON or XML error message in the HTTP body containing an error message and an error code.

Write access: Create, update and delete operations map to the standard HTTP verbs (POST, PUT, DELETE) against the entity set. They are implemented by redefining the corresponding methods (CREATE_ENTITY, UPDATE_ENTITY, DELETE_ENTITY) in the same data provider class. The content of the respective data set is sent in the HTTP body.

Other features: OData v2 comes with built-in query options such as filtering on specific fields, selecting data by key or regular fields, and paging. In SEGW, however, most of these must be implemented manually in the data provider classes. On the output side, both XML and JSON are supported, with JSON being the de facto default in most implementations today. OData v2 also provides a service description in the form of an EDMX file following the Common Schema Definition Language (CSDL), which can be retrieved by appending $metadata to the service root.

When to use it: OData v2 via SEGW is stable, and many systems rely on it, but it is no longer where SAP’s strategic development effort goes. For new services, SAP steers toward RAP. Note that RAP can also expose services via OData v2, so "OData v2" and "SEGW" are not strictly the same decision.

 

4. Custom REST (ICF handler)

How it works: This option builds on a rather basic framework: a handler class is registered directly in the Internet Communication Framework (SICF). The handler class acts as a dispatcher. It interprets incoming calls and selects and executes a suitable resource class. There is no metadata, no generated create/read/update/delete (CRUD) functionality and no standardized query syntax. The developer decides on the URL structure, the payload shape, the HTTP verbs used, and how (or whether) to support filtering and paging, down to the interpretation and setting of each individual HTTP header. This makes it the most flexible option covered here, and also the one with the least built-in support.

Implementation: The starting point is a handler class implementing the interface IF_HTTP_EXTENSION. This class interprets the service-specific part of the URI and matches it against registered patterns, similar to regular expressions. When the URI matches a pattern, the resource class registered for that pattern is called. Patterns can contain variables, for instance /client/{clientid: [1-9][0-9]*}. A call ending in /client/4711 would invoke the registered resource class with the parameter clientid set to 4711.

The resource class must implement the interface IF_REST_RESOURCE, in which the methods for the individual HTTP verbs can be redefined (e.g. IF_REST_RESOURCE~GET). Inside these methods, the variables from the URI are available, as well as other inputs such as HTTP headers, the HTTP body and query parameters. After parsing these, the business logic is executed, and the HTTP status code, response headers and response body are set by the custom code.

Example call: Since there is no protocol convention to follow, the shape is entirely up to the developer. A call might look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/bc/zbp_address/Partner/P1001

Accept: application/json

Error handling: Also entirely custom: the development team decides which HTTP status codes to return and how to structure the error body.

Write access: No different in principle from read access. The development team handles the HTTP verbs and payload parsing, and is fully responsible for locking, transactional consistency and validation, since none of the generic RAP or Gateway services apply here.

Other features: Features such as filtering or paging must be implemented from scratch. The response format is entirely free (JSON, XML or anything else). The response body is serialized manually, for JSON for example often with the class /ui2/cl_json.

When to use it: This option is most sensible when a use case genuinely doesn’t fit the standard interfaces, for example because of a highly custom payload shape, a non-CRUD-style API, or a need for tight control over the exact response format. It comes, however, at the price of conceptualizing and implementing a lot of different features that come for free elsewhere.

 

5. RAP (ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model) / OData v4

RAP is SAP’s current strategic model for building services, and the one most closely tied to the Clean Core principle in S/4HANA and to ABAP Cloud. Rather than a single technology, RAP is better understood as a framework with one standard implementation style (managed) and two custom implementation styles (custom entity and unmanaged). These styles differ substantially in how much the framework does and how much has to be implemented by hand. All three are introduced together here because they share the same tooling and core concepts.

5.1 Standard (managed) RAP

How it works: This is the standard way of developing in RAP. Core Data Services (CDS) view entities are defined and connected, and a behavior definition marked as managed is added on top. The framework then generates features such as CRUD from declarative annotations, so no read, create or update methods have to be written by hand.

Implementation: The foundation is a virtual data model made up of CDS views along two dimensions. The first dimension consists of three layers of views defined by SAP: basic views, composite views and consumption views. The second dimension is the relationships between the business entities in those views. In the running example, three basic views are created to access the tables BUT000, BUT020 and ADRC. On the interface layer, two views are created: Z_I_PARTNER and Z_I_PARTNER_ADDRESS. The first reads from the BUT000 basic view, while the second joins the data from BUT020 and ADRC. The two interface views are linked by a composition reflecting the parent-child relationship between partner and address. To expose the model, two consumption views are created which are based on the interface views and restrict the exposed fields to only the one’s necessary in the interface. Next, a behavior definition turns the entity model into a business object (BO) by annotating it with a set of keywords describing its features (see below). Finally, a service definition exposes the relevant entities, and a service binding (UI or Web API, OData v2 or v4) makes the service callable from outside. Note that the whole implementation can be done without writing any ABAP code: only CDS views and configuration artifacts are created. However, adding operations on top of CRUD is possible as determinations and actions using ABAP.

Example call: The shape of read access depends on whether OData v2 or v4 is chosen in the service binding. An OData v4 example could look like this:

GET https://<system>.example.com/sap/opu/odata4/sap/zsb_address_v4/srvd/sap/zsd_address/0001/BusinessPartnerAddress('P1001')

Accept: application/json

Error handling: As with SEGW, errors come back as standard HTTP status codes, accompanied by an OData-standard message in the HTTP body containing an error message and an error code.

Write access: Write capabilities are added declaratively through annotations in the behavior definition. This covers create, update and delete, as well as transaction handling and the ability to save draft versions.

Other features: Standard RAP comes with a wide range of built-in features, which are either active by default or can be added via annotations in the behavior definition. Some of them are: (1) paging, including the use of a skip token, (2) automatic generation of key values for new entries, (3) lock handling for concurrent write processes, (4) authorization handling on different levels, (5) automatic switching between XML and JSON response formats (for OData v2).

When to use it: This is the technology SAP actively recommends for new S/4HANA development, and the one best aligned with Clean Core extensibility. If one is starting from scratch and the interface required is about exposing data consisting of different linked entities based on database tables (as opposed to interfaces with rather algorithmic nature), this is the default choice. It does require a change in thinking about interfaces: Instead of one endpoint for each part or angle of the data in a traditional input-output setup, a data model for a whole domain can be exposed. If that model is well structured, many different data needs can be fulfilled simply through the right OData parameters of one interface endpoint. Parameterizing the requests can be a challenge of it’s own, though, because deciding which entities to read, with which fields, in which order and for which filter criteria, can get very complex.

5.2 RAP with custom entity

How it works: Sometimes data doesn’t come from a straightforward CDS view over a database table. It might come from an RFC call to another system, from a computed result, or from a BAPI wrapping complex logic. A custom entity keeps the consistency of RAP and OData (same tooling, same protocol, same annotation model) while the data retrieval is implemented by hand.

Implementation: The entity’s attributes are defined in a custom-entity CDS definition, marked with the annotation @ObjectModel.query.implementedBy, which names a custom ABAP class. Note that, unlike regular CDS views, a custom entity does not rely on a database table or another view. The ABAP class implements the interface IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER. The signature of its method provides all OData parameters sent by the caller, so it is the developer's duty to handle these parameters and to retrieve and return the result data. The custom entity is then exposed through a behavior definition (in this case optional), a service definition and a service binding, just as with standard entities.

Comparison with standard RAP: With a custom entity, the RAP framework still receives and parses the call’s parameters, but reacting to them is up to the developer’s own ABAP logic. Most OData features therefore remain available in principle, but most of them must be programmed manually. This is also why mixing custom and standard entities within a complex virtual data model can be very challenging and is in some cases impossible. A second limitation is that managed custom entities are read-only. For custom RAP developments with write access, unmanaged business objects are the right choice.

When to use it: A useful complement to standard RAP for read-only scenarios in which standard RAP cannot be used. Where possible, however, prefer exposing the full data model over single, isolated custom entities.

5.3 Unmanaged RAP

How it works: This style provides full control over a business object, including all write operations. The data model can be defined with regular CDS views or custom entities. In contrast to managed RAP, however, the transactional behavior (create, update, delete, locking, authorization and saving) is not generated by the framework but implemented manually.

Implementation: The data model is built from regular CDS views or custom entities just as in managed RAP. In the behavior definition, the business object is then marked as unmanaged together with the name of an implementation class. This class contains local classes: one inheriting from CL_ABAP_BEHAVIOR_HANDLER, in which the methods for creating, updating, deleting, locking and authorizations are implemented, and a second one inheriting from CL_ABAP_BEHAVIOR_SAVER, which gives full control over the LUW transaction handling and the actual saving of the data.

Comparison with standard RAP: Compared to standard RAP or custom entities, unmanaged business objects offer the maximum control over functionality, at the cost of considerably more implementation effort. In this respect they are roughly comparable to the custom REST approach described above. The difference is that a custom REST handler is a very loose framework in which almost everything is a free decision, whereas unmanaged business objects come with a much stricter framework. That framework can act as a guardrail for the implementation, but it can also mean implementing functionality the project does not actually need.

Where this stands today: Valid and supported, but with meaningfully more implementation effort than managed RAP. It should be a deliberate choice for cases that need the control, not a default.

7. Conclusion

The comparison shows that the further one moves from SOAP or Custom REST toward managed RAP, the more the framework takes over and the less control (and boilerplate code) remains for the developer. This reflects the typical trade-off between flexibility and framework support that is inherent in virtually every programming framework.

In line with SAP’s recommendation, RAP, and in particular standard (managed) RAP, should be the strategic default for new, Clean-Core-aligned services on S/4HANA. It is also the area into which SAP directs its tooling and documentation efforts. The other technologies nevertheless remain relevant in specific situations. SOAP-released BAPIs are the fastest way to expose functionality that already exists as a function module, and given their widespread use in existing landscapes, it is unlikely that they will disappear simply because SAP no longer recommends them. OData v2 via SEGW is a reasonable choice when extending an existing Gateway-based landscape. Finally, a custom REST service based on an ICF handler remains an option for requirements that fit no standardized model at all. It trades standardization, such as metadata, paging and error conventions, for flexibility, and this trade-off should be a deliberate decision.

Within RAP, standard RAP, custom entity and unmanaged business objects are not competing alternatives but tools for different situations. Standard RAP is best suited to exposing an entire data model of several interconnected entities with few or no algorithmic requirements. A custom entity is appropriate when the data cannot easily be derived from CDS views over database tables and only needs to be read. An unmanaged business object keeps the CDS-based model but replaces the generated transactional behavior with custom logic. It therefore fits cases in which write operations do not match the generated CRUD model, for example when they involve many case distinctions or the reuse of existing function modules. In each case, the choice follows the same principle: the more of the implementation is taken over by custom logic, the more control is gained, and the more of the framework’s support is given up.
